It then checks a seven-way equality chain: the bank must be keyed to the stage-1 checkpoint and gene space, the gate metadata to stage-1, stage-2, gene space, and the bank's fingerprint, and retrieval settings must agree between gate and bank ([morph2mol/release.py](/morph2mol/release.py#L23-L46)). Inside the model itself, the stage-2 checkpoint records the SHA-256 of the stage-1 initializer and a gene-order hash, both re-verified at load ([predict/model.py](/predict/model.py#L22-L29)). The consequence: any mismatched mixture of checkpoints, genes, bank, and weights fails fast at startup instead of producing silently wrong predictions.

Sources: [morph2mol/release.py](/morph2mol/release.py#L6-L46), [predict/model.py](/predict/model.py#L22-L29)

## Where to Go Next

- Component internals: [Image Encoder and LoRA Adapters](6-image-encoder-and-lora-adapters), [SE(2) Distance Attention Decoder](7-se-2-distance-attention-decoder), [Negative-Binomial Expression Head](8-negative-binomial-expression-head), [scGPT RNA Embedding Backend](9-scgpt-rna-embedding-backend)

# Image Encoder and LoRA Adapters



This page explains how Morph2Mol converts a 224×224 cell crop into a 1536-dimensional morphological feature vector. The design pairs a **completely frozen UNI2-h vision transformer** (~700M parameters) with a small set of **LoRA adapters** (roughly 1.77M trainable parameters) injected into its attention projections. You will learn how the backbone is constructed and verified, how the adapters are mathematically defined and injected, how patch tokens are pooled into per-cell vectors, and how adapter weights travel through the two-stage training pipeline into a release artifact that supports hot-swapping between the two trained adapter states.

Sources: [encoder.py](/morph2mol/encoder.py#L1-L41), [predict/model.py](/predict/model.py#L1-L48)

## Architecture at a Glance

The encoder subsystem follows a strict separation: the backbone is immutable, adaptation is confined to attention layers, and all parameter movement happens through explicit, shape-checked checkpoints. Every pixel-level decision (normalization constants, token prefix handling, mask pooling) lives in a single shared module used identically by training and inference — the module's own docstring states it provides "UNI2-h and LoRA utilities shared by training and inference" ([encoder.py](/morph2mol/encoder.py#L1)).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Input["Cell Crop Pipeline"]
        CROP["uint8 crop [B,3,224,224]<br/>resized bilinear"]
        NORM["(x/255 - MEAN) / STD<br/>ImageNet stats"]
    end
    subgraph UNI2H["UNI2-h ViT-Huge (frozen, ~700M)"]
        PATCH["Patch embed 14×14<br/>+ CLS + 8 register tokens"]
        BLOCKS24["24 Transformer blocks<br/>SwiGLU MLP, dim 1536"]
        subgraph Adapted["Blocks 12–23: attention adapted"]
            QKV["attn.qkv = LoRALinear"]
            PROJ["attn.proj = LoRALinear"]
        end
        FEATS["forward_features<br/>[B, 265, 1536]"]
    end
    POOL["Mask-weighted token pooling<br/>skip 9 prefix → 16×16 grid → w16 weighted sum"]
    OUT["Cell feature [B, 1536]"]

    CROP --> NORM --> PATCH --> BLOCKS24 --> FEATS --> POOL --> OUT
    BLOCKS24 -.-> Adapted
    QKV -.-> PROJ
```

Two numbers anchor the parameter-efficiency story. The trainable surface consists of 12 adapted blocks × 2 projections × 2 matrices (A and B) = **48 adapter tensors**. With rank r=16 on `qkv` (1536→4608) and `proj` (1536→1536), each block contributes 147,384 parameters, giving 1,768,608 trainable parameters in Stage 1 — about 0.25% of the backbone.

Sources: [encoder.py](/morph2mol/encoder.py#L17-L21), [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L11-L19), [stage1.py](/morph2mol/training/stage1.py#L139-L141)

## The Frozen UNI2-h Backbone

The backbone is instantiated through `build_uni2_local`, which constructs a `vit_huge_patch14_224` from timm with UNI2-h's specific configuration and loads weights from a local directory — never from an online hub — using a **strict shape check** (`strict=True` in `load_state_dict`). This guarantees the release weights match the architecture bit-for-bit in shape before any adapter work begins. After loading, every parameter is set to `requires_grad = False` and the model is moved to the device in `eval()` mode, so the backbone can never drift during training or inference.

| Construction argument | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `img_size` / `patch_size` | 224 / 14 | 14×14 grid = 256 patch tokens |
| `depth` / `num_heads` / `embed_dim` | 24 / 24 / 1536 | ViT-Huge capacity |
| `mlp_layer` / `act_layer` | `SwiGLUPacked` / `SiLU` | Gated SwiGLU feed-forward |
| `mlp_ratio` | 2.66667 × 2 | SwiGLU effective expansion (~5.33×) |
| `reg_tokens` | 8 | 8 register tokens alongside CLS |
| `init_values` | 1e-5 | Layer-scale initialization |
| `no_embed_class` / `dynamic_img_size` | True / True | Flexible input sizing support |

Three module-level constants complete the backbone contract: `MEAN`/`STD` hold ImageNet normalization statistics applied as `(x/255 - MEAN)/STD`, and `PREFIX = 9` counts the tokens skipped during pooling (1 CLS + 8 register tokens), leaving exactly the 256 patch tokens per crop.

Sources: [encoder.py](/morph2mol/encoder.py#L6-L8), [encoder.py](/morph2mol/encoder.py#L29-L40)

> [!TIP]
> The `strict=True` load in `build_uni2_local` is a deliberate integrity barrier: if the local `pytorch_model.bin` does not exactly match the timm architecture (including the 8 register tokens), construction fails immediately rather than producing a silently mis-aligned encoder downstream.

## LoRA Adapter Design

`LoRALinear` wraps any frozen `nn.Linear` and adds a low-rank residual path. The wrapper freezes the base weights at construction time (`p.requires_grad = False`), then registers two parameters: **A** of shape `(r, in_features)` initialized with Kaiming-uniform (a=√5), and **B** of shape `(out_features, r)` initialized to **zeros**. The forward pass is:

```
output = base(x) + (dropout(x) @ Aᵀ @ Bᵀ) × s,    where s = alpha / r
```

Because B starts at zero, the adapter contributes exactly nothing at initialization — the adapted model is numerically identical to the frozen backbone at the start of Stage 1, and gradients flow only through the low-rank path. With the recipe values alpha=32 and r=16, the scale factor is s = 32/16 = **2.0**, and dropout of 0.05 is applied to the adapter's input branch only.

The injection point is surgical: `inject_lora` replaces `attn.qkv` and `attn.proj` in the **last `nblocks` blocks only** (iterating `range(n - nblocks, n)`). All feed-forward layers, embeddings, and the first 12 blocks remain untouched — the model retains its pretrained visual semantics while the deepest attention layers gain capacity to specialize on histology-style crops.

| Projection | Base Linear | A shape (r=16) | B shape (r=16) | Adapter params |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `attn.qkv` | 1536 → 4608 | 16 × 1536 | 4608 × 16 | 98,232 |
| `attn.proj` | 1536 → 1536 | 16 × 1536 | 1536 × 16 | 49,152 |
| **Per block** | — | — | — | **147,384** |
| **12 blocks (Stage 1)** | — | — | — | **1,768,608** |
| **9 blocks (Stage 2 trainable)** | — | — | — | **1,326,456** |

Sources: [encoder.py](/morph2mol/encoder.py#L9-L21), [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L11-L19)

> [!TIP]
> The zero-initialized B matrix is what makes the trainable-parameter digest meaningful: `stage1.py` hashes every `requires_grad` tensor at initialization (`init_hash`), and because adapters start at a deterministic identity state, this digest binds each checkpoint to its exact initialization — a mismatch aborts resume ([training_resume.py](/morph2mol/training_resume.py#L117-L118)).

## Mask-Weighted Token Pooling

The bridge from transformer tokens to a per-cell vector is `pooled_feat`, which implements what the code calls the "recipe cmask pool". It takes the full feature sequence `[B, 265, 1536]` from `forward_features`, discards the first `PREFIX = 9` tokens, reshapes the remaining 256 patch tokens into a 16×16 spatial grid (computed as `round(256 ** 0.5)`), and performs a **weighted average** against a per-cell mask weight tensor `w16` of shape `[B, 16, 16]` whose rows sum to 1. The result is one 1536-dimensional vector per cell, weighted toward the tokens covered by the cell's actual nucleus/membrane footprint rather than an uninformative global average.

The `w16` tensors are produced upstream by rasterizing each cell's polygon boundary at full crop resolution and area-averaging down to the 16×16 token grid, with a documented degenerate fallback: if a polygon rasterizes to an effectively empty mask (`w.sum() <= 1e-6`), a delta weight at the center token `(8, 8)` is substituted so pooling remains well-defined. This same pooling path serves both the contrastive tower path (`he_embed`) and the expression model path, guaranteeing identical spatial semantics in both training stages and at inference.

Sources: [encoder.py](/morph2mol/encoder.py#L22-L28), [contrastive.py](/morph2morph/../training/contrastive.py#L50-L64), [contrastive.py](/morph2mol/training/contrastive.py#L45-L48)

## Adapter Lifecycle: Stage 1 → Stage 2

The adapters are not trained once — they are trained **twice with different scopes**, and the checkpoint format records exactly which tensors each stage owns. This lifecycle is the single most important thing to understand about this subsystem.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph S1["Stage 1 — Contrastive Alignment (3 epochs)"]
        A1["inject_lora(12, 16, 32, 0.05)<br/>all 48 A/B tensors trainable"]
        A2["AdamW lr=1.5e-4, warmup 150 steps<br/>InfoNCE vs scGPT cell embeddings"]
        A3["stage1 checkpoint: lora = trainable(model)<br/>→ complete 48-tensor set"]
    end
    subgraph S2["Stage 2 — Expression Training (3 epochs)"]
        B1["load stage-1 lora (complete=True)"]
        B2["re-enable all A/B, then freeze_first_lora:<br/>freeze first 3 of 12 adapted blocks<br/>→ 36 trainable tensors"]
        B3["AdamW lr=3e-5 + grad checkpointing<br/>stage2 checkpoint: lora = trainable subset (36)"]
    end
    subgraph INF["Inference — Morph2Mol"]
        C1["inject_lora(args from ckpt)"]
        C2["load stage-1 lora complete=True (48)"]
        C3["overlay stage-2 lora (36)"]
        C4["frozen blocks 12–14 carry Stage-1 weights;<br/>blocks 15–23 carry Stage-2 weights"]
    end
    A1 --> A2 --> A3 --> B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> C1 --> C2 --> C3 --> C4
```

In **Stage 1**, `inject_lora(model, 12, 16, 32, 0.05)` makes all 48 adapter tensors trainable, optimized with AdamW at lr 1.5e-4 (towers at 1e-3, weight decay 0.01) with linear warmup over the first 150 steps. Checkpoints store `lora=C.trainable(model)` — precisely the requires-grad set, i.e., the complete 48-tensor collection ([stage1.py](/morph2mol/training/stage1.py#L171-L176)).

In **Stage 2**, the encoder is rebuilt, the stage-1 checkpoint is validated as a *completed* three-epoch run, and its LoRA set is loaded with `complete=True` ([stage2.py](/morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L144-L148)). All 48 tensors are then re-enabled and `freeze_first_lora` immediately freezes `A`/`B` of the **first three** of the twelve adapted blocks — matching the recipe's `freeze_frac=0.2` (3/12). The remaining 36 tensors continue training at lr 3e-5 with gradient checkpointing enabled for memory. The stage-2 checkpoint therefore contains only the 36-tensor trainable subset: `lora={n: p.detach().cpu() for ... if p.requires_grad}` ([stage2.py](/morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L218-L223)).

| Property | Stage 1 | Stage 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Injected blocks | last 12 (indices 12–23) | last 12 (same geometry) |
| Trainable adapters | 48 (all A/B) | 36 (blocks 15–23; blocks 12–14 frozen) |
| Learning rate | 1.5e-4 | 3e-5 |
| Loss objective | InfoNCE (temperature 0.07) | Negative-binomial NLL + MSE |
| Checkpoint `lora` contents | complete 48-tensor set | 36-tensor trainable subset |
| Initialization binding | `init_hash` over trainable init | `stage1_identity` (sha256 of stage-1 ckpt) |

Sources: [stage1.py](/morph2mol/training/stage1.py#L139-L155), [stage1.py](/morph2mol/training/stage1.py#L193-L194), [stage2.py](/morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L98-L104), [stage2.py](/morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L150-L153), [stage2.py](/morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L167-L169), [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L22-L33), [contrastive.py](/morph2mol/training/contrastive.py#L41-L43)

> [!TIP]
> Because stage-2 checkpoints save only the 36-tensor trainable subset, inference must load in a fixed order: stage-1 first with `complete=True` (filling all 48), then stage-2 as an overlay. The code comments this explicitly — "Stage-2 saves only the trainable subset; frozen adapters still come from Stage-1" ([predict/model.py](/predict/model.py#L45-L46)) — so blocks 12–14 run with contrastive-alignment weights while blocks 15–23 carry expression-tuned weights.

## The LoRA Loading Contract

Every adapter load in the codebase — training resume, stage-2 initialization, and inference — funnels through one function: `load_lora_checked`. Its contract has four clauses, each with an explicit failure mode:

1. **Key whitelist**: every provided name must end in `.A` or `.B` and must exist among the encoder's parameters (`expected`); anything outside is rejected.
2. **Non-empty**: an empty tensor dict is rejected outright.
3. **Completeness flag**: with `complete=True`, the provided set must exactly equal the expected 48-name set — used when a stage claims to own the full adapter state.
4. **Shape equality**: each tensor's shape must match the live parameter exactly, catching rank/config drift before any weight is written.

Only after all checks pass does it call `load_state_dict(tensors, strict=False)`, which is safe precisely because the pre-validation already established a perfect key/shape match ([training_contract.py](/morph2mol/training_contract.py#L68-L77)).

At inference, `Morph2Mol.__init__` assembles this into a verification chain: the encoder is built and adapted using hyperparameters read from the stage-2 checkpoint's `args` (`nblocks`, `lora_r`, `lora_alpha`, `lora_dropout`), the fixed Morph2Mol-25M recipe is enforced via `check_stage2_settings` (which compares every recipe key against the checkpoint), the stage-2 checkpoint's `stage1_identity.sha256` is compared against the release's stage-1 hash to prove both stages came from the same lineage, and the gene head hash guards output-space consistency — then the two-phase LoRA load proceeds ([predict/model.py](/predict/model.py#L13-L41), [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L36-L39)).

The assembled model also supports **adapter hot-swapping**: `encode` accepts `which='stage2'` (default) or `which='phase1'`, and on switch it copies the retained stage-1 or stage-2 tensors into the live parameters ([predict/model.py](/predict/model.py#L50-L55)). This lets consumers extract either the expression-tuned geometry or the contrastive-alignment embedding space from a single loaded release. Encoding itself is chunked (default 64 crops per chunk) under autocast bf16/fp16, taking uint8 crops in `[N, 3, 224, 224]` layout and returning float32 `[N, 1536]` features ([predict/model.py](/predict/model.py#L56-L62)). A `Voice25M = Morph2Mol` alias preserves compatibility for existing inference adapters ([predict/model.py](/predict/model.py#L71-L73)).

Sources: [training_contract.py](/morph2mol/training_contract.py#L68-L77), [predict/model.py](/predict/model.py#L13-L62), [training_resume.py](/morph2mol/training_resume.py#L131-L135)

## Configuration Reference

The recipe module locks the adapter hyperparameters as fixed settings — callers may only supply runtime arguments (paths, workers, chunk size, save interval, resume), and any attempt to override a recipe key raises a `TypeError` at construction ([recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L11-L19)).

| Parameter | Value | Applies to | Defined in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nblocks` | 12 | Both stages | [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L15), [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L26) |
| `r` / `lora_r` | 16 | Both stages | [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L15), [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L26) |
| `alpha` / `lora_alpha` | 32 (scale s = 2.0) | Both stages | [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L15), [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L26) |
| `dropout` / `lora_dropout` | 0.05 | Both stages | [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L15), [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L26) |
| `lr_lora` (Stage 1) | 1.5e-4, warmup 150 | Stage 1 | [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L14) |
| `lr_lora` (Stage 2) | 3e-5, `grad_ckpt=True` | Stage 2 | [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L27) |
| `freeze_frac` | 0.2 (3 of 12 blocks) | Stage 2 | [recipe.py](/morph2mol/recipe.py#L27) |
| `PREFIX` / `MEAN` / `STD` | 9 / ImageNet stats | Pooling & normalization | [encoder.py](/morph2mol/encoder.py#L6-L8) |

## Where to Go Next

The 1536-d features produced here feed directly into the rest of the model: the [SE(2) Distance Attention Decoder](7-se-2-distance-attention-decoder) consumes them via a 1536→256 projection and spatial transformer, and the [Negative-Binomial Expression Head](8-negative-binomial-expression-head) maps the decoded cell states to gene expression. For the training objectives that shaped these adapters, see [Stage 1 Contrastive Alignment](14-stage-1-contrastive-alignment) and [Stage 2 Expression Training](15-stage-2-expression-training); for how adapter checkpoints become a verified release artifact, see [Model Export and Release Packaging](17-model-export-and-release-packaging).

# SE(2) Distance Attention Decoder



This page dissects the spatial decoder that sits between Morph2Mol's frozen image encoder and the negative-binomial expression head. The decoder — a six-layer stack that conditions attention on pairwise cell distances measured in microns — is what turns a bag of independent per-cell image embeddings into a spatially coherent set of cell representations. We cover its role in the pipeline, the block geometry that feeds it, the Gaussian distance basis, the layer internals, its geometric invariance properties, and the training/checkpoint contract that pins it to the released 25M checkpoint. Throughout, `B` denotes the number of cells in a block (targets + context), `N` is a generic cell count, `d_model = 256`, `d_pair = 64`, and `n_heads = 8`.

Sources: [se2.py](morph2mol/se2.py#L1-L22), [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L1-L2), [recipe.py](morph2mol/recipe.py#L22-L33)

## Role in the Inference Pipeline

The released `Morph2Mol` class composes exactly three trainable stages after the encoder: a 1536→256 projection (`inp`), the `SpatialTransformer` (`se2`), and the `DirectHead` (`head`). The decoder consumes projected, mask-pooled UNI2-h features (one 256-dim token per cell) plus micron-resolution centroid coordinates, and emits one 256-dim spatial embedding per cell that the expression head converts into per-gene negative-binomial means. At inference, `decode()` returns both `log1p(mu)` (the direct prediction written to `layers['A']`) and the spatial embedding `z` (optionally persisted as `obsm['X_morph2mol_se2']`).

Sources: [model.py](predict/model.py#L36-L41), [model.py](predict/model.py#L64-L68), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L149-L153)

Prerequisite: the diagram below shows the full decode path — all arrows into the decoder come from the encoder stage documented in [Image Encoder and LoRA Adapters](6-image-encoder-and-lora-adapters), and the arrow out goes to the head documented in [Negative-Binomial Expression Head](8-negative-binomial-expression-head).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["H&E cell crops<br/>(B × 3 × 224 × 224)"] --> B["UNI2-h encoder<br/>+ LoRA adapters"]
    B --> C["Mask-pooled features<br/>(B × 1536)"]
    C --> D["inp: Linear 1536→256"]
    E["Centroids in microns<br/>pos (B × 2)"] --> F["GaussianModule<br/>pairwise distances → pair features Z<br/>(B × B × 64)"]
    D --> G["SpatialTransformer<br/>6 × SE2Layer(d=256, pair=64, heads=8)"]
    F --> G
    G --> H["LayerNorm(256)<br/>z (B × 256)"]
    H --> I["DirectHead<br/>NB means μ (B × G)"]
    I --> J["log1p(μ) → layers['A']"]
```

Sources: [model.py](predict/model.py#L64-L68), [se2.py](morph2mol/se2.py#L7-L21), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L139-L141)

> [!TIP]
> The decoder is invoked **per spatial block, never per slide**: `decode()` receives `pos_um[indices]` for one target+context block (≤192 cells), so the pairwise tensor is small and O(B²) attention is cheap — but the micron unit is load-bearing. Training converts pixel positions with `um_per_pixel_source` (`pos = pos_px * ums`), and inference multiplies source pixels by `mpp`; feed pixel coordinates instead and every normalized distance lands far outside the Gaussian basis's `[0, 137] µm` calibration, clamping to `1.0` and silently collapsing the distance signal.

Sources: [training/stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L40-L41), [covariates.py](predict/covariates.py#L35-L36), [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L14)

## Spatial Block Geometry: Targets and Context Halos

The decoder never sees a whole slide at once. Both training and inference use the identical partitioning machinery from `full_coverage.py`: cells are assigned to blocks of at most 128 target cells, and each block is augmented with up to 64 context (halo) cells found within a 137 µm radius. The fixed recipe constants — `TARGET_CELLS = 128`, `CONTEXT_CELLS = 64`, `RADIUS_UM = 137.0` — are shared by both stages and are enforced at checkpoint load time, so the released model cannot be run with different block geometry.

Sources: [recipe.py](morph2mol/recipe.py#L4-L8), [recipe.py](morph2mol/recipe.py#L23-L27), [spatial_context.py](predict/spatial_context.py#L20-L26)

**Partitioning** (`partition_cells`) is deterministic and epoch-parameterized: cells are rotated by a random angle drawn uniformly from `[−π/4, π/4]`, projected onto a jittered square grid sized so that blocks average the target budget, then recursively bisected along their widest axis until every block holds ≤ 128 cells. An assertion verifies every cell is owned exactly once per epoch. Training re-partitions each epoch (seed + `epoch*1000003`), while inference pins `epoch=0` and derives the partition seed from `crc32(sample_id)`, making output partitioning a fixed function of the sample identity.

Sources: [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L14-L40), [spatial_context.py](predict/spatial_context.py#L24-L26), [README.md](README.md#L57)

**Halo selection** (`halo_cells`) queries a `cKDTree` for the `k=16` nearest neighbors of each target, filters to candidates within the 137 µm radius that are not already targets, deduplicates, and takes the first 64. The block fed to the model is `targets ‖ context` — a single prefix-ordered index array where the first `n_targets` rows are owned targets and the remainder is context. Note that this halo is *nearest-neighbor-bounded*, not radius-guaranteed: if a target's 16 nearest neighbors all sit inside its own block, no halo cells arise from that target.

Sources: [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L43-L52), [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L113-L126), [spatial_context.py](predict/spatial_context.py#L32-L40)

## The Pair Distance Basis: GaussianModule

All geometric information enters the decoder through one tensor: the pairwise distance matrix `D[i,j] = ‖pos_i − pos_j‖`. `GaussianModule(d_pair=64, n_gaussians=128, max_dist=137.0)` converts distances into pair features in three steps. First, distances are divided by the 137 µm cutoff and clamped to `[0, 1]`. Second, each normalized distance is expanded against 128 learnable Gaussian basis functions with parameters `means ∈ [0,1]` (initialized as `linspace(0, 1, 128)`) and `log_stds` (initialized to zero, i.e. unit width, with a `1e-4` floor after exponentiation). Third, the 128-dim basis vector is linearly projected down to `d_pair = 64`. The basis configuration of the production checkpoint is `GaussianModule(64, 128, 137.0)` — 64 pair channels, 128 RBF centers, 137 µm saturation — exactly matching `RADIUS_UM`.

Sources: [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L5-L17), [se2.py](morph2mol/se2.py#L10), [recipe.py](morph2mol/recipe.py#L7)

| Component | Shape / value | Initialization | Learnable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Input distances `D` | `B × B` | — | — |
| Normalized `D/max_dist` | `B × B`, clamped `[0,1]` | `max_dist = 137.0` | No |
| Gaussian means | 128 | `linspace(0, 1, 128)` | Yes |
| Gaussian log-stds | 128 | zeros (σ = 1) | Yes |
| Projection `proj` | 128 → 64 | — | Yes |
| Output pair features `Z` | `B × B × 64` | — | — |

Sources: [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L6-L17), [se2.py](morph2mol/se2.py#L10)

## Anatomy of One SE2Layer

Prerequisite: each `SE2Layer(256, 64, 8)` maintains **two coupled tracks** — a node track `feat` (`B × 256`) and a pair track `Z` (`B × B × 64`). The pair track starts as pure geometry (Gaussian distance encoding) but is progressively rewritten: every layer lets cell appearance refine the pair state, then converts the refined pair state into per-head attention biases. The diagram traces one layer's forward pass.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph inputs["Layer inputs"]
        F["feat (B×256)"] --> N1["norm1"]
        Z["Z (B×B×64)"] --> NP["norm_pair"]
    end
    N1 -- "outer sum feat_i + feat_j" --> PU["pair_update: Linear 256→8<br/>(B×B×8)"]
    PU --> CAT["concat → 72 dims"]
    NP --> CAT
    CAT --> MLP["pair_mlp: 72→64 GELU 64→64"]
    MLP -- "residual" --> Z2["Z ← Z + ΔZ"]
    Z2 --> PB["pair_to_bias: 64→8<br/>permute → (8×B×B)"]
    N1 --> QKV["q/k/v projections<br/>8 heads × 32 dims"]
    QKV -- "scores/√d + bias" --> SM["softmax → bmm(attn, V)"]
    PB --> SM
    SM --> OUT["out_proj → residual into feat"]
    OUT --> FF["norm2 → FFN 256→1024→256 → residual"]
    FF --> FN["(feat′, Z′) → next layer"]
```

Sources: [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L41-L57)

Three design decisions deserve attention. First, the **pair update is content-conditioned**: `pair_update(norm(feat_i) + norm(feat_j))` projects the *sum of node features* into 8 channels, concatenated onto the 64 pair channels and pushed through a gated residual MLP (`pair_mlp`). Pair features therefore encode "distance + what the two cells look like", not distance alone. Second, the **attention bias path** projects the pair tensor to `n_heads` logits via `pair_to_bias` and adds them to scaled dot-product scores before softmax — structurally equivalent to Graphormer-style spatial biasing, but with a bias that is itself a learned, evolving function of both geometry and appearance. Third, the layer is fully **pre-normalized** (three LayerNorms: `norm1` on nodes entering attention and pair update, `norm_pair` on the pair tensor, `norm2` before the 4×-expanded GELU FFN), with residuals on both the node output projection and the FFN, which keeps the six-layer stack stable under the 1e-4 learning rate.

Sources: [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L29-L39), [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L43-L57)

> [!TIP]
> The pair tensor `Z` is **mutable state threaded through the whole stack** — `SpatialTransformer.forward` reassigns `x, Z = layer(x, Z)` six times, and `SE2Layer` returns the updated `Z` alongside the features. The `GaussianModule` only *initializes* this state; after layer one, the attention bias reflects accumulated geometry-appearance interactions, not raw distances. This is also why `broadcast_buffers=False` is safe during DDP training: there are no buffers to synchronize, and every parameter that matters is replicated and all-reduced through gradients.

Sources: [se2.py](morph2mol/se2.py#L15-L21), [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L45-L47), [training/stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L172-L173)

## SpatialTransformer Composition and Cost

`SpatialTransformer` stacks six identical `SE2Layer(256, 64, 8)` modules — three in a `pre` list and three in a `post` list — executed back-to-back with no architectural difference between the groups, matching the recipe's `n_layers=6`. The forward pass computes the distance matrix once per block, initializes `Z`, runs the six layers, and applies a final `LayerNorm(256)`. Summing the projection shapes yields roughly **4.8M parameters** (≈ 801K per SE2 layer × 6, plus ≈ 8.5K for the Gaussian module and 512 for the output norm) — a small fraction of the 25M-parameter checkpoint, whose bulk lives in the UNI2-h LoRA adapters and the expression head.

Sources: [se2.py](morph2mol/se2.py#L7-L21), [recipe.py](morph2mol/recipe.py#L25-L26)

| Tensor | Where produced | Shape (block of B cells) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pooled image features | encoder + mask pooling | `B × 1536` |
| Projected node tokens | `inp` Linear | `B × 256` |
| Pairwise distances `D` | `forward` norm | `B × B` |
| Pair features `Z` (init) | `GaussianModule` | `B × B × 64` |
| Per-head attention logits | `pair_to_bias` | `8 × B × B` |
| Output embedding `z` | `norm_out` | `B × 256` |

Sources: [se2.py](morph2mol/se2.py#L15-L21), [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L47-L54), [model.py](predict/model.py#L36-L38)

Cost scales with the square of block size. At the maximum block composition of 128 targets + 64 context (B = 192), the pair tensor holds 192 × 192 × 64 ≈ 2.4M activations, attention logits hold 8 × 192 × 192 ≈ 295K per layer, and every cell in the block — targets and context alike — attends to all 192 cells with no masking between the two populations. The encoder, by contrast, processes cells in independent chunks (`--enc-chunk`, default 64), so the decoder is the only component whose receptive field spans the block.

Sources: [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L119-L121), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L24-L25), [model.py](predict/model.py#L50-L62)

## Why "SE(2)": Geometric Invariance by Construction

SE(2) is the special Euclidean group of the plane — translations and rotations. The decoder earns its name because the **only** geometric quantity that influences attention is `‖pos_i − pos_j‖`, and the norm of a displacement vector is invariant under both translations and rotations of the coordinate frame. Slide the entire cell constellation to a new origin, or rotate the tissue, and every Gaussian basis activation, every pair feature, and consequently every attention bias is unchanged (up to feature-space effects via content-conditioned pair updates, which themselves are permutation-equivariant). The module docstring states the design directly: "Morph2Mol SE(2) distance attention, as used by the 25M checkpoint," over "Six spatial attention layers using pairwise distances in microns."

Sources: [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L1), [se2.py](morph2mol/se2.py#L1)

The training data pipeline actively reinforces this invariance. Because `partition_cells` rotates all positions by a fresh random angle in `[−π/4, π/4]` every epoch before grid assignment, the decoder is trained on block compositions drawn from continuously re-rotated coordinate frames — the pairing of cells inside a block changes with rotation even though cell identity does not. Combined with the distance-only attention bias, this yields a decoder whose spatial behavior does not depend on the scanner's orientation convention, which matters when inference-time partitions (fixed at epoch 0, seeded by sample ID) are generated for arbitrarily oriented slides.

Sources: [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L17-L26), [spatial_context.py](predict/spatial_context.py#L24-L26)

One subtlety: invariance applies to the *geometry pathway*, not the whole layer. The outer-sum pair update uses node features derived from H&E crops, which carry their own orientation statistics. The distance bias is frame-invariant; the appearance pathway is merely insensitive to cell order. This is a deliberate pragmatic trade — full equivariant message passing (steerable kernels, irreducible representations) would cost considerably more compute for a 6-layer, 256-dim stack.

Sources: [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L44-L45)

## Training Dynamics and the Checkpoint Contract

During Stage 2, the decoder is part of `ExpressionModel` alongside `inp` and `DirectHead`, and trains under a distinct learning-rate group: the `rest` parameter group (everything except encoder LoRA) — which includes the entire `SpatialTransformer` — uses `lr = 1e-4`, matching the recipe's `lr_se2=1e-4`, while LoRA adapters move at `3e-5`. Weight decay is zero, gradients are globally clipped at norm 1.0, and forward/backward runs under `autocast` (the decoder receives `h.float()` projected features, so its own math is fp32 inside the autocast boundary of the encoder).

Sources: [training/stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L80-L91), [training/stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L167-L169), [recipe.py](morph2mol/recipe.py#L27), [training/stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L189-L200)

Supervision is prefix-masked: `supervised_sums` applies both the negative-binomial NLL and the `log1p`-scale MSE **only to the target prefix** of each block, while context cells participate fully in attention but contribute zero loss — they exist purely to inform the targets' spatial embeddings. The dataset returns an explicit boolean mask (`mask = arange(len(idx)) < len(targets)`, zeroed for invalid slots under multi-rank schedules), and per-epoch assertions verify that exactly `cells × epochs` targets were supervised.

Sources: [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L119-L121), [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L129-L138), [training/stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L191-L197), [training/stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L202-L208)

The released decoder is pinned by a multi-layer contract. Checkpoints store `se2=model.se2.state_dict()` next to `inp` and `head`; `check_stage2_settings` rejects any checkpoint whose args deviate from the fixed recipe on keys including `d_model=256`, `n_layers=6`, `max_dist=137.0`, `target_cells=128`, and `context_cells=64`; and `Morph2Mol.__init__` loads `inp`, `se2`, and `head` with `strict=True` after verifying the stage-1 initializer identity and gene-head hash. In short: a released checkpoint and the decoder code must agree on shapes, layer count, and distance calibration, or inference refuses to start.

Sources: [training/stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L218-L223), [recipe.py](morph2mol/recipe.py#L36-L40), [model.py](predict/model.py#L23-L29), [model.py](predict/model.py#L39-L41)

## Outputs, Observability, and Failure Guards

The decoder's output feeds two destinations. The primary path hands `z` to `DirectHead`, whose returned means are transformed to `log1p(mu)` and written to the `layers['A']` dataset of the streaming `.h5ad`; a nonfinite guard (`np.isfinite(direct).all()`) aborts the run rather than writing corrupt rows. The secondary path is diagnostic: with `--save-embeddings`, the raw 256-dim spatial embeddings are persisted as `obsm['X_morph2mol_se2']` in float16, alongside stage-2 image embeddings and phase-1 retrieval embeddings. At inference, `commit_target_rows` scatters **only the target prefix** of each block's decoder outputs into slide-global arrays exactly once, while context rows — predicted redundantly in overlapping blocks — are always discarded.

Sources: [model.py](predict/model.py#L65-L68), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L150-L159), [spatial_context.py](predict/spatial_context.py#L64-L78), [README.md](README.md#L106-L107)

## Key Takeaways

The SE(2) decoder is best summarized as a Graphormer-shaped transformer whose positional encoding is a learnable Gaussian RBF over micron distances, wrapped in a content-conditioned pair track that mutates across six pre-norm layers. Its block-level operating regime (128 targets + 64 halo cells within 137 µm) is identical at train and inference time and enforced by the checkpoint contract; its spatial invariance comes from distance-only biasing plus per-epoch random partition rotations; and its ~4.8M parameters are optimized at `lr_se2=1e-4` against prefix-masked NB NLL + MSE losses.

Sources: [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L5-L57), [recipe.py](morph2mol/recipe.py#L4-L8), [training/stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L167-L197)

| Property | Value | Where enforced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Layers / width / heads | 6 × SE2Layer(256, 64, 8) | `se2.py` + `check_stage2_settings` |
| Distance calibration | 137 µm cutoff, 128 Gaussian bases | `GaussianModule(64, 128, 137.0)` |
| Block composition | ≤128 targets + ≤64 context | recipe constants + partition/halo code |
| Decoder parameters | ≈ 4.8M (derived from shapes) | module definitions |
| Supervision | target prefix only; NB NLL + MSE | `supervised_sums` mask |
| Output | `log1p(mu)` (A layer) + 256-dim `z` | `decode()` |

Sources: [se2.py](morph2mol/se2.py#L7-L21), [_se2_arch.py](_se2_arch.py#L5-L17), [recipe.py](morph2mol/recipe.py#L36-L40)

## Where to Go Next

To understand what the decoder's 256-dim output is *for*, continue to [Negative-Binomial Expression Head](8-negative-binomial-expression-head), which documents the `DirectHead` gene projection and area covariates. For the block-partition and halo machinery shared with fused inference, see [Spatial Context Blocking](19-spatial-context-blocking); for the training loop that optimizes the decoder, see [Stage 2 Expression Training](15-stage-2-expression-training); and for how the stage-2 embeddings branch into retrieval-based fusion, see [Cluster Retrieval Mechanics](11-cluster-retrieval-mechanics). The broader component layout is covered in [Architecture Overview](5-architecture-overview).


# Negative-Binomial Expression Head



This page documents the expression head that converts SE(2) cell latents into per-gene expected counts under a negative-binomial observation model. It covers the `DirectHead` module, the `nb_nll` likelihood, the cell-area covariates that modulate predictions, and the contracts that keep this component identical during Stage-2 training and inference.

## Role in the Prediction Stack

The head is the last stage of the Morph2Mol prediction pipeline and the only component that emits expression values. Upstream, an H&E cell crop and its mask pass through the image encoder with LoRA adapters to yield a 1,536-d pooled feature; a linear projection compresses this to 256 dimensions, and the SE(2) spatial transformer mixes neighborhood positions into a cell latent `z`. The head then maps `z`, two scalar area covariates, and a gene-row selection into a vector of expected counts `mu`, which is exported as `log1p(mu)` in the `layers/A` matrix of the output `.h5ad`. Prerequisites: the diagram below assumes you know that pooled features come from the encoder and that the SE(2) decoder consumes micron positions — both are detailed in [SE(2) Distance Attention Decoder](7-se-2-distance-attention-decoder).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["H&E crop + mask"] --> B["Image encoder\n+ LoRA (autocast bf16)"]
    B --> C["Pooled feature\n(1536-d)"]
    C --> D["Linear inp\n1536 -> 256"]
    D --> E["SE(2) spatial transformer\n(neighbor positions)"]
    E --> Z["Cell latent z (256-d)"]
    Z --> H["DirectHead MLP\n258 -> 1024 -> D"]
    AR["area_abs, area_rel"] --> H
    H --> L["logit = z' @ W[head_idx]ᵀ + b[head_idx]"]
    L --> M["mu = softplus(logit) + 1e-4"]
    M --> AE["mu × (area/median)^γ"]
    AE --> OUT["log1p(mu) → layers/A"]
```

The same wiring appears twice in the codebase with identical semantics: `ExpressionModel` during training composes `enc → inp → se2 → head`, and the portable `Morph2Mol.decode` mirrors exactly `se2(inp(features), positions)` followed by the head call. This duplication is deliberate — inference never imports the training drivers.

Sources: [stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L80-L91), [model.py](predict/model.py#L64-L68), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L121-L122), [head.py](morph2mol/head.py#L1)

## DirectHead Anatomy

`DirectHead` holds three kinds of state: **learnable gene rows**, a **covariate MLP**, and **area/dispatcher scalars**. Its docstring is a precise summary: "Learnable scGPT gene rows, cell area covariates and a global area exponent." The `E` buffer stores the frozen initial scGPT gene-embedding table `[G, D]`, while `W` is a same-shaped trainable parameter initialized as a clone of `E` — the recipe's `free_head=True, free_init='emb'` options. The per-gene bias `b` starts at zero, `log_gamma` is a scalar in log space controlling the global area exponent, and `log_theta` is a per-gene vector of log inverse-dispersion values.

| Parameter | Shape | Initialization | Trainable | Role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `E` (buffer) | `[G, D]` | scGPT gene embeddings | No (frozen anchor) | Initial-value record; fixes `G` and `D` |
| `W` | `[G, D]` | Clone of `E` | Yes | Projection rows from cell latent to gene logit |
| `mlp` | 258→1024→D | LayerNorm + Linear + GELU + Linear | Yes | Fuses cell latent with two area covariates |
| `b` | `[G]` | Zeros | Yes | Per-gene bias on the logit |
| `log_gamma` | scalar | 0 | Yes | Log of the global area exponent γ |
| `log_theta` | `[G]` | Zeros | Yes | Log per-gene NB inverse dispersion |

Two dimensions are structural rather than learned: the MLP input width **258** is the recipe's `d_model` (256) plus exactly two area covariates, and `D` is taken from the scGPT gene-embedding table loaded from `gene_emb_scgpt.npz`. Stage-2 asserts that the table's gene order matches the model gene space before construction, so `W`'s rows are permanently bound to that ordering.

Sources: [head.py](morph2mol/head.py#L24-L34), [stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L154-L157), [recipe.py](morph2mol/recipe.py#L22-L33), [training.md](docs/training.md#L88-L96)

## Forward Pass: From Latent to Expected Counts

The forward pass is four steps, each with a deliberate numerical safeguard. First, the cell latent `h` is concatenated with the stacked `[area_abs, area_rel]` pair and pushed through the MLP to produce `z`. Second, only the rows of `W` and `b` selected by `head_idx` participate in the projection — during training `head_idx` maps the slide's measured gene symbols to global model-gene rows; at inference it is the user-requested panel. Third, the logit passes through `softplus` plus a `1e-4` floor, guaranteeing a strictly positive mean rate `mu` so downstream `log1p` and ratio terms stay finite. Fourth, a multiplicative size factor scales `mu` by `exp(exp(log_gamma) · area_rel)` per cell.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Head["DirectHead.forward"]
        Z["z = MLP( cat(h, [area_abs, area_rel]) )"] --> P["logit = z @ W[head_idx].T + b[head_idx]"]
        P --> S["mu = softplus(logit) + 1e-4"]
        S --> G["mu × exp(exp(log_gamma) · area_rel)"]
    end
    G --> NLL["nb_nll(y, mu, exp(log_theta)) — training only"]
    G --> EXP["log1p(mu) — exported at inference"]
```

The row-selection design has a practical consequence: `W` and `b` span the full gene space, but a prediction of arbitrary width (all genes, the Xenium subset, or a custom list) touches only the requested rows, so panel size affects compute, not the model. The `softplus` choice means `mu` is smooth in the logit with non-vanishing gradients at zero counts, which matters because single-cell count matrices are extremely sparse.

Sources: [head.py](morph2mol/head.py#L36-L40), [stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L52-L59), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L102-L105)

## Cell-Area Covariates and the Learned Size Law

Larger cells capture more transcripts, so raw expected counts must scale with segmented cell area. The head consumes two covariates derived from nucleus/cell polygon geometry: `area_abs = log(area + 1)` and `area_rel = log(area + 1) − log(median + 1)`, where the median is computed per slide over cells with positive area. During training, `cell_areas` reads `patch_cell_boundaries.npz`, converts polygon vertices to µm² using the `(55 / output_size)²` patch-frame scale, and applies the shoelace formula. Degenerate polygons (fewer than three vertices) are replaced by the slide median — never zero — which prevents a silently collapsed area signal.

The inference path computes the identical covariates in `predict/covariates.geometry`, whose docstring explicitly names the parity target: "the covariates expression_head.cell_areas / LiveStore build." The two implementations agree on scale conversion, log transforms, median estimation, and degenerate-polygon fallback, making the covariate contract symmetric across training and deployment.

| Property | Training (`cell_areas` / `LiveStore`) | Inference (`geometry`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source geometry | `patch_cell_boundaries.npz` vertices in patch frame | Segmentation or prepared-slide polygons |
| Area units | Shoelace × `(55/output_size)²` µm² | Shoelace × `mpp²` µm² (rescaled to output frame) |
| Absolute covariate | `log(area + 1)` | `log(area + 1)` |
| Relative covariate | `log(area + 1) − log(med + 1)` | `log(area + 1) − log(med + 1)` |
| Degenerate polygons | Slide median replacement | Slide median replacement; 60 µm² default if none positive |

> [!TIP]
> At initialization `log_gamma = 0`, so the area factor reduces exactly to `exp(area_rel) = area/median` — the head *starts* with a linear area-scaling law and training only learns the exponent γ of the power law `mu ∝ (area/median)^γ`. This is why the docstring calls it a "global area exponent": one scalar governs all genes, initialized to the physically sensible linear regime.

Sources: [head.py](morph2mol/head.py#L7-L22), [stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L67-L69), [covariates.py](predict/covariates.py#L14-L36)

## The Negative-Binomial Likelihood

`nb_nll` implements the exact negative-binomial log-likelihood for observed count `y`, mean `mu`, and inverse dispersion `θ = exp(log_theta)`: `lgamma(θ) + lgamma(y+1) − lgamma(y+θ) + θ·log1p(μ/θ) + y·log1p(θ/μ)`. This is the standard NB negative log-likelihood after expanding the normalization constant — the two `log1p` terms are the rewritten log-probability masses `(θ/(θ+μ))^θ` and `(μ/(θ+μ))^y`. Unlike a Poisson head, the per-gene dispersion lets the model tolerate the over-dispersion of single-cell counts: low-`θ` genes get a flatter likelihood, which damps gradient pressure toward their noisy means.

Numerical discipline is baked into the call sites. The dispersion is clamped to `[1e-4, 1e4]` after exponentiation, and training indexes it by `head_idx` so only measured genes contribute their `log_theta` entries to the loss. Note the asymmetry of roles at deployment: `log_theta` shapes training gradients only — the exported quantity is `mu`, so dispersion never appears in prediction outputs, it exists purely to regularize how each gene's mean is learned.

| Loss ingredient | Feeds from head | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NB NLL (primary) | `mu`, `log_theta[head_idx]` | Likelihood of raw integer counts; dispersion-aware |
| log1p MSE (auxiliary) | `mu` | Stabilizes optimization on log-scale targets; equal weight per recipe |
| Uniform cell weights | — | Placeholder vector; `wg.sum()` normalization in `supervised_sums` |

Sources: [head.py](morph2mol/head.py#L42-L45), [stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L187-L198), [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L129-L138)

## Training Integration in Stage 2

Stage 2 wraps the head in `ExpressionModel` and trains it for three epochs with complete target-cell coverage. Each optimization step processes a spatial block of up to 128 owned target cells plus up to 64 halo context cells within 137 µm; a boolean mask marks the target rows so context cells participate in SE(2) attention but contribute zero loss — enforced inside `supervised_sums`, which slices both losses to masked rows and normalizes by the weight sum. The combined step loss is `nll·scale + mse·scale`, where `nll` and `mse` are block means over owned cells and `scale = world/count` rescales by the cross-rank supervised count.

Parameter grouping separates the head from the encoder: LoRA adapters train at `lr=3e-5` while the `rest` group — `inp`, `se2`, and every head parameter including `log_theta` and `log_gamma` — trains at `lr=1e-4` with zero weight decay. Checkpointing binds the head to the corpus through two hashes written into the checkpoint: `gene_head_sha256` (SHA-256 of the ordered gene symbol list) and the Stage-1 checkpoint identity, and resume restores `head` with `strict=True` so no parameter can silently drift.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    B["Block: ≤128 targets + ≤64 halo cells"] --> F["ExpressionModel forward → mu"]
    F --> MASK["mask: context rows dropped"]
    MASK --> L1["nb_nll(y, mu, log_theta[hi]) → mean"]
    MASK --> L2["log1p MSE → mean"]
    L1 --> TOT["(nll + mse) × world/count"]
    L2 --> TOT
    TOT --> BW["backward → clip 1.0 → AdamW step"]
    BW --> CK["atomic save: head state + gene_head_sha256"]
```

The training recipe fixes every hyperparameter the head depends on — `d_model=256`, equal loss weights (`lam_aux=lam_mse=1.0`), `gene_emb='scgpt'`, `free_head=True`, `free_init='emb'` — and `check_stage2_settings` rejects any checkpoint that deviates, so released heads are guaranteed to be the Morph2Mol-25M configuration. The broader optimization loop, coverage rotation, and resume mechanics are covered in [Stage 2 Expression Training](15-stage-2-expression-training) and [Resume, Caching, and Reproducibility](16-resume-caching-and-reproducibility).

Sources: [stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L167-L169), [stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L187-L208), [stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L211-L223), [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L108-L126), [recipe.py](morph2mol/recipe.py#L26-L39)

## Inference and Release Integration

The released model reconstructs the head without the training corpus, under a strict identity contract. `Morph2Mol.__init__` verifies that the Stage-2 checkpoint's recorded `stage1_identity.sha256` matches the release's Stage-1 hash, that `gene_head_sha256` matches the hash of the loaded gene space, and that all recipe settings pass `check_stage2_settings` — only then is a `DirectHead` constructed and its state loaded with `strict=True`. Any mismatch in gene order, adapter lineage, or recipe aborts before a single prediction is made.

> [!TIP]
> The head is instantiated as `DirectHead(np.zeros(ck['head']['E'].shape))` — at inference, the `E` buffer's *contents* are irrelevant; only its shape is needed to size the parameter set before the strict state-dict load overwrites everything. Combined with the `gene_head_sha256` binding, this makes gene-order drift structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged.

At decode time the head receives the SE(2) latent, the geometric covariates, and the panel row indices, returning `log1p(mu)` together with `z` for optional embedding export. The direct predictions stream into `layers/A` of the output `.h5ad` block by block, with a finiteness guard that hard-fails on any nonfinite value before disk write. The metadata records the scale explicitly (`A_scale: 'log1p(mu)'`), and downstream fusion reads `A` as the direct branch of `beta·A + (1−beta)·R` — that mechanism is documented in [Gated Fusion Weights](12-gated-fusion-weights), and the output format in [Reading Prediction Outputs](4-reading-prediction-outputs).

| Inference contract | Enforcement point |
| --- | --- |
| Stage-2/Stage-1 lineage | `stage1_identity.sha256` vs release hash |
| Gene ordering | `gene_head_sha256` vs `gene_hash(genes)` |
| Recipe identity | `check_stage2_settings` on saved args |
| State completeness | `load_state_dict(..., strict=True)` |
| Numeric validity | Per-block `np.isfinite(direct).all()` guard |

Sources: [model.py](predict/model.py#L21-L47), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L117-L159), [training_contract.py](morph2mol/training_contract.py#L39-L40), [release.py](morph2mol/release.py#L22-L26)

## Design Summary

Three properties define this head's engineering character. **Positivity by construction**: softplus with a floor and a clamped dispersion mean the likelihood is always evaluable, even for degenerate cells or extreme logits. **Parity by duplication**: training and inference compute covariates through separate but semantically identical code paths, with the inference docstring naming the training implementation as its reference. **Identity by hashing**: the head's gene rows are welded to an ordered gene space via SHA-256, checked at every resume, export, and load. Together these let a 46-line module carry a production guarantee usually associated with far larger subsystems.

To continue through the model components, follow the natural dependency order: [SE(2) Distance Attention Decoder](7-se-2-distance-attention-decoder) for the latent producer, [scGPT RNA Embedding Backend](9-scgpt-rna-embedding-backend) for the source of the `E` initialization, then [Stage 2 Expression Training](15-stage-2-expression-training) for the full optimization context and [Model Export and Release Packaging](17-model-export-and-release-packaging) for how the head's checkpoint becomes a portable artifact.


# scGPT RNA Embedding Backend



The scGPT RNA Embedding Backend is Morph2Mol's vendored, minimal re-implementation of the scGPT foundation model's encoder, used exclusively to **prepare RNA embedding targets for training** — it never loads during image inference. This page explains the three backend components (`model.py`, `preprocess.py`, `data_collator.py`), the checkpoint-bridging technique that loads pretrained scGPT weights into stock PyTorch layers, and the offline pipeline (`train/embed_scgpt.py`) that converts raw expression matrices into L2-normalized cell embeddings. Understanding this backend is prerequisite context for [Stage 1 Contrastive Alignment](14-stage-1-contrastive-alignment), where these embeddings serve as the alignment targets for the image pathway described in [Image Encoder and LoRA Adapters](6-image-encoder-and-lora-adapters).

Sources: [NOTICE.md](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/NOTICE.md#L1-L6), [model.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/model.py#L1-L2)

## Role in the System: An Offline Teacher, Not a Runtime Dependency

Morph2Mol predicts gene expression from morphology images, but to *train* that prediction it needs ground-truth RNA representations. Rather than aligning image embeddings directly against raw count vectors, the system first projects each cell's measured expression profile through a pretrained scGPT transformer, producing a semantically rich cell embedding in which genes are contextualized against the model's learned transcriptomic prior. These embeddings become the fixed, non-trainable "RNA side" of the contrastive objective.

The design deliberately isolates this role. The module docstring calls it an encoder used "to prepare Morph2Mol-25M RNA targets," and NOTICE.md states plainly that "image inference does not load scGPT." This isolation is enforced at the dependency level: `requirements-train.txt` contains no scGPT package — the needed components are vendored directly into `morph2mol/scgpt_backend/` under MIT license — so the lean inference environment never carries transformer-training baggage. Consequently, every artifact that ships to end users (the release model, prediction CLI) is free of this code path; only the training-preparation tooling touches it.

Sources: [model.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/model.py#L1-L2), [NOTICE.md](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/NOTICE.md#L1-L6), [requirements-train.txt](/requirements-train.txt#L1-L3)

## Module Anatomy and Licensing

The backend is deliberately compact — three source files plus attribution documents, 164 lines of Python in total:

| File | Lines | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| `model.py` | 67 | `GeneEncoder`, `ContinuousValueEncoder`, `TransformerModel` — the encode-only architecture |
| `preprocess.py` | 70 | Quantile `binning` of expression values into discrete bins |
| `data_collator.py` | 27 | Batch assembly: binning, length capping, subsampling, padding |
| `LICENSE` / `NOTICE.md` | 22 / 6 | MIT license from scGPT (Copyright 2022, suber / bowang-lab) and adaptation provenance |

NOTICE.md attributes the components to **scGPT 0.2.4** and records the two deviations that matter for auditing: the RNA embedding model and collator were adapted for training-target preparation, and the expression binning was retained to match scGPT's original discretization convention. The MIT license permits this vendoring without copyleft obligations on Morph2Mol itself.

Sources: [NOTICE.md](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/NOTICE.md#L1-L6), [LICENSE](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/LICENSE#L1-L2), [model.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/model.py#L1-L67), [preprocess.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/preprocess.py#L1-L70), [data_collator.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/data_collator.py#L1-L27)

## Model Architecture: Two Embeddings, One Transformer

The architecture follows scGPT's signature pattern — each gene position in a cell's sequence carries two pieces of information: *which* gene it is (categorical identity) and *how much* of it is expressed (continuous magnitude). Two parallel encoders project these into a shared `d_model`-dimensional space, the projections are **summed element-wise**, and the fused token sequence flows through a standard transformer stack. A padding mask (`src_key_padding_mask`) keeps padded positions out of attention computations.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    G["Gene ID tokens<br/>(batch, seq_len)"] --> GE["GeneEncoder<br/>nn.Embedding + LayerNorm"]
    V["Expression values<br/>(batch, seq_len)"] --> CV["ContinuousValueEncoder<br/>clamp ≤ 512 → Linear(1→d) → ReLU<br/>→ Linear(d→d) → LayerNorm → Dropout"]
    GE --> SUM(("⊕<br/>sum"))
    CV --> SUM
    SUM --> TE["nn.TransformerEncoder × nlayers<br/>d_model / nhead / d_hid, batch_first<br/>src_key_padding_mask"]
    TE --> CLS["Position 0 holds ⟨cls⟩<br/>→ cell embedding (batch, d_model)"]
```

The two encoders embody contrasting inductive biases. `GeneEncoder` is a plain `nn.Embedding` lookup over the vocabulary followed by `LayerNorm`, with `padding_idx` bound to the vocabulary's pad token so pad positions receive a fixed null embedding. `ContinuousValueEncoder` is a small MLP that treats each scalar expression value independently: it clamps values at `max_value=512` (bounding outliers), projects the scalar through `Linear(1→d_model)` with ReLU, then `Linear(d_model→d_model)`, normalizes, and applies dropout.

Sources: [model.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/model.py#L7-L23), [model.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/model.py#L25-L52), [model.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/model.py#L55-L67)

### Encode-Only by Design

`TransformerModel` exposes a single method, `_encode(src, values, src_key_padding_mask)`, and defines **no `forward`**. This is not an omission — it is a statement of scope. The full scGPT release ships generative heads and training objectives; Morph2Mol only ever needs contextual embeddings, so the vendored class stops at the transformer encoder's output. The constructor wires the scGPT checkpoint's hyperparameters straight through (`ntoken`, `d_model`, `nhead`, `d_hid`, `nlayers`, `dropout`, `pad_token`) and uses PyTorch's built-in `nn.TransformerEncoderLayer` with `batch_first=True` rather than a custom attention implementation — a choice whose consequences become central in the checkpoint-loading section below.

Sources: [model.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/model.py#L55-L67), [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L22-L24)

## Expression Binning: From Counts to 51 Discrete Levels

scGPT does not feed raw expression magnitudes to the value encoder; it feeds **quantile-binned levels**, and Morph2Mol preserves that convention exactly. The vendored `binning(row, n_bins)` computes `n_bins - 1` quantile edges over the row and digitizes each value into one of `n_bins` levels. Because quantile edges can collide when data concentrates, the helper `_digitize` handles ties explicitly: it digitizes from both the left and right, then linearly interpolates with a uniform random draw and applies `ceil` — spreading identical values *uniformly across the tied bins* instead of dumping them all at one edge.

The function also hardens against degenerate inputs, with distinct behaviors worth knowing when inspecting binning diagnostics:

| Input condition | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Entire row is zero | Logs a warning; returns a zero row (preserving dtype) |
| Row contains zeros or negatives | Quantile edges computed over **non-zero values only**; zeros/negatives pinned to bin 0 |
| Strictly positive row | Quantile edges over all values |
| Values tied across a bin edge | Randomized `ceil` assignment between left/right digitize results |

Note the asymmetry in the zero-handling branch: only values above zero participate in quantile estimation, so an expression of 0 maps to level 0 regardless of the distribution of positive values — matching scGPT's semantics where zero expression is a distinct, absolute state.

Sources: [preprocess.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/preprocess.py#L36-L70), [preprocess.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/preprocess.py#L7-L34)

## The DataCollator Contract

`DataCollator` turns variable-length cell records into uniform tensors, applying four rules in sequence. It first caps the batch's sequence length at `min(1200, longest example in batch)` — a hard memory ceiling. It then bins the expression values into **51 levels**, but critically it applies binning to `values[1:]` only: position 0 is the reserved `<cls>` slot whose expression value is never discretized. For over-length examples, it subsamples by drawing a `randperm` over positions 1…L−1 and always concatenating position 0 first — the CLS token survives every subsample. Short examples are right-padded with the pad token ID and pad value.

| Step | Rule | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Length cap | `min(1200, max(len(genes)))` across batch | Bounded peak memory |
| Binning | `binning(values[1:], n_bins=51)` — skips index 0 | scGPT's 51-level discretization; CLS slot exempt |
| Subsampling | `randperm` over positions ≥ 1; position 0 always kept | Gene diversity per epoch; CLS anchor preserved |
| Padding | Append `pad_token_id` genes + `pad_value` expressions | Uniform `(B, L)` tensors |

The output dictionary — `{'gene': stacked ids, 'expr': stacked values}` — deliberately drops per-example identity information. That choice shapes the consumption code downstream: since the collator discards which cell came from which row, the pipeline must recover cell identity from the batch sampler's ordering, as shown in the pipeline section.

Sources: [data_collator.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/data_collator.py#L8-L27), [data_collator.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/data_collator.py#L1-L3)

> [!TIP]
> The CLS slot at index 0 is protected through the entire stack: it is excluded from 51-bin discretization, excluded from random subsampling, and seeded with `pad_value` as its expression. This invariant is what allows the embedding read-out to blindly take position 0's output as *the* cell representation.

## Checkpoint Loading: The QKV Bridge

The pretrained scGPT checkpoint (`best_model.pt`) was trained with a custom attention module whose fused query-key-value projection is named `Wqkv`. PyTorch's stock `nn.TransformerEncoderLayer` stores the same mathematics split as `in_proj_weight` and `in_proj_bias`. `load_model` bridges this gap with a one-line state-dict key rewrite — every key beginning `Wqkv.` is renamed to begin `in_proj_` — after which the weights slot directly into the PyTorch layer. Without this remap, a naive `load_state_dict` would silently skip *all* attention weights.

Because arbitrary checkpoint keys may not match, the loader uses `strict=False` with a shape-filtered intersection (only tensors whose names and shapes both match are accepted). This permissiveness is then fenced in by a hard completeness assertion: every key of the model's own state dict under `encoder.`, `value_encoder.`, or `transformer_encoder.` must appear among the loaded tensors, or the loader raises with the first five missing names. The net effect is a loader that tolerates checkpoint cruft (heads, buffers, aux modules) but cannot proceed with a partially-loaded encoder. Configuration comes from `args.json` (`embsize`, `nheads`, `d_hid`, `nlayers`, `dropout`, `pad_token`, `pad_value`) and `vocab.json`, with upfront assertions that the special tokens `<pad>`, `<cls>`, and `<eoc>` all exist in the vocabulary.

> [!TIP]
> The `strict=False` + completeness-assertion pattern is worth reusing: it converts "load whatever matches" from a silent-partial-load risk into an explicit, diagnostic-rich failure — you get the count of matched tensors logged, and a hard stop naming any missing encoder tensor.

Sources: [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L17-L34), [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L25-L33)

## The Embedding Pipeline: From CSR Matrix to Normalized Targets

`train/embed_scgpt.py` orchestrates the full conversion. It discovers every object directory under `dataset/training_set/{xenium,cosmx}/*/*` containing an `expression.npz`, skips already-cached outputs, supports `--only` filtering and `--shard/--nshard` splitting for parallel workers, and processes each object through the flow below.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Discover objects in<br/>training_set/{xenium,cosmx}"] --> B{"output .npy<br/>already cached?"}
    B -- "yes" --> Z["skip"]
    B -- "no" --> C["Load expression.npz CSR<br/>+ genes.tsv symbol column"]
    C --> D["Map symbols → vocab IDs<br/>keep in-vocab columns only"]
    D --> E["Seed numpy: crc32(object name)<br/>torch.manual_seed(0)"]
    E --> F["CellDS: per-cell CSR row slice<br/>genes + positive values,<br/>prepend ⟨cls⟩ at pad_value"]
    F --> G["Sort cells by non-zero count,<br/>pack token-budget batches ≤ 98,304"]
    G --> H["DataCollator: 51-bin binning,<br/>cap 1200, pad to uniform"]
    H --> I["model._encode under no_grad<br/>+ fp16 autocast on CUDA"]
    I --> J["Take position 0 output →<br/>L2-normalize → float16"]
    J --> K["Atomic write .tmp.npy → os.replace<br/>+ per-object metrics .json"]
```

Three implementation details inside this flow deserve attention. **Gene-space intersection**: each platform's measured panel is projected onto the scGPT vocabulary via `vocab.get(symbol, -1)`; genes outside the vocabulary are dropped column-wise before embedding, and the log line reports how many of the panel's genes survived. **Per-cell extraction**: `CellDS` reads one CSR row at a time, filters to strictly positive values, and prepends the `<cls>` token ID at position 0 with `pad_value` as its expression — the collator's binning of `values[1:]` then leaves this slot untouched. **Identity recovery**: because the collator discards cell IDs, the loop indexes into the precomputed `batches` list positionally (`batches[k]`) to map each returned embedding back to its cell row in the output matrix.

Sources: [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L93-L126), [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L51-L64), [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L65-L84)

### Token-Budget Batching

Rather than fixed-size batches, cells are sorted by their non-zero gene count (stable sort, empty cells filtered out) and greedily packed so that `(batch size) × (longest cell in batch)` never exceeds `max_tokens` (default 98,304). Each cell's contribution is bounded at `min(nnz, 1199) + 1` tokens — 1,199 genes plus the CLS slot — aligning with the collator's 1,200-token cap. Length-sorting minimizes padding waste within a batch, which is where fixed-size batching over heavy-tailed cell-gene distributions loses most of its throughput.

Sources: [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L65-L73), [data_collator.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/data_collator.py#L10)

### Output Post-Processing and Persistence

After inference, each cell's CLS-position embedding is L2-normalized (rows with zero norm are left as zeros rather than divided by ~0) and cast to **float16**, halving storage for what will become training targets. Results are written per object as `{object}.npy` alongside a metrics JSON (`n_cells`, in-vocab gene count, non-zero statistics, cells that were subsampled, wall time). The write is atomic — save to `.tmp.npy`, then `os.replace` — which is what makes the cache-existence check in the main loop safe across interrupted runs and parallel shard workers.

The CLI surface is intentionally minimal:

| Flag | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `--dataset` | required | Corpus root containing `training_set/{xenium,cosmx}` |
| `--scgpt-dir` | required | Checkpoint directory (`args.json`, `vocab.json`, `best_model.pt`) |
| `--out` | required | Output directory for per-object `.npy` + metrics `.json` |
| `--only` | *(all)* | Comma-separated object names; unknown names hard-fail |
| `--shard` / `--nshard` | 0 / 1 | Stride-based partitioning across parallel workers |
| `--max_tokens` | 98304 | Token budget per batch |
| `--workers` | 8 | DataLoader worker processes |

Sources: [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L76-L90), [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L106-L125), [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L94-L101)

## Determinism by Construction

Randomness enters this pipeline in exactly two places — the tie-spreading draws in `_digitize` and the `randperm` subsampling in the collator — and both are pinned. NumPy is seeded with `zlib.crc32(object_name)`, a choice annotated in the code itself: Python's built-in `str` hash is salted per process, so it cannot serve as a reproducible seed, whereas CRC32 is stable across processes and machines. Torch is seeded to 0. The consequence: re-running `embed_scgpt.py` on the same object reproduces bit-identical embeddings, which matters because these targets feed a contrastive objective where silent target drift between resume runs would corrupt alignment training. This complements the broader resume and caching machinery described in [Resume, Caching, and Reproducibility](16-resume-caching-and-reproducibility).

Sources: [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L61-L62), [preprocess.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/preprocess.py#L28-L33)

## Design Decisions and Trade-offs

The backend's shape follows from a few deliberate engineering choices, summarized here:

| Decision | Rationale | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Vendor 3 files instead of importing `scgpt` package | Zero heavyweight dependency; inference installs stay lean | Manual reconciliation against upstream scGPT releases |
| Stock `nn.TransformerEncoderLayer` | Standard weight layout, no custom attention to maintain | Requires the `Wqkv.` → `in_proj_` key remap at load time |
| Encode-only API (`_encode`, no `forward`) | Embeddings are read-only training targets | Cannot reuse the class for generative scGPT tasks |
| Per-object `.npy` + JSON sidecar | Row-aligned targets; embedded provenance metrics | Many small files rather than one consolidated store |
| float16 storage of targets | Halves disk footprint for large corpora | Negligible precision loss after L2 normalization |
| CRC32 object-name seeding | Process-stable, machine-stable reproducibility | Tied to object names; renaming changes subsampling |

Sources: [requirements-train.txt](/requirements-train.txt#L1-L3), [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L26-L33), [model.py](/morph2mol/scgpt_backend/model.py#L64-L66), [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L85-L90), [train/embed_scgpt.py](/train/embed_scgpt.py#L61-L62)

## Where the Embeddings Go Next

Each output `.npy` is row-aligned with the object's cells: row *i* of the embedding matrix corresponds to `expr_rows` entry *i* in the object's `patch_cell_boundaries.npz`, the contract that lets training join every image crop to its RNA target. From there, these frozen embeddings become the fixed anchor in Stage 1's contrastive objective — the image pathway learns to point at them.

For the natural reading progression from here:

- [Stage 1 Contrastive Alignment](14-stage-1-contrastive-alignment) — how image embeddings are trained against these RNA targets
- [Training Data Contracts](13-training-data-contrats → [Training Data Contracts](13-training-data-contracts)) — the exact row-alignment and crop-to-expression join semantics
- [Reference Bank Construction](10-reference-bank-construction) — how expression-derived geometry feeds retrieval at inference time
- [Model Export and Release Packaging](17-model-export-and-release-packaging) — why none of this backend ships to end users


# Reference Bank Construction



The reference bank is Morph2Mol's retrieval substrate: a compact, fingerprinted store of clustered (image-feature, measured-expression) summaries derived from training reference slides. At inference, direct model predictions are fused with expression retrieved from this bank, so its construction determines both the quality and the reproducibility of every prediction. This page explains how the bank is built — from encoding reference slides to writing verified on-disk artifacts — and why each step is structured the way it is. Retrieval-time behavior is covered in [Cluster Retrieval Mechanics](11-cluster-retrieval-mechanics), and how the resulting weights are fitted is covered in [Gated Fusion Weights](12-gated-fusion-weights).

The system's purpose frames everything below: predict spatial gene expression from H&E images using "an image encoder, a spatial decoder, and a reference bank of cells with measured expression" [README.md](/README.md#L1-L3). The bank ships with the downloadable model, alongside checkpoints, fusion weights, and gene information [README.md](/README.md#L14-L20).

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L3), [README.md](/README.md#L14-L20)

## Where the Bank Sits in the Architecture

Bank construction is a post-training, pre-inference step. It consumes an intermediate release (containing the Stage-1 alignment checkpoint and gene space but not yet the bank or gate) and produces a directory of per-reference cluster summaries that a final release packages by reference. The two modules involved have a clean producer/consumer split:

- **`train/prepare_bank.py`** — encodes each reference slide through the full prediction pipeline and materializes per-cell features and expression as plain NumPy arrays plus a manifest.
- **`morph2mol/bank_builder.py`** (exposed as `predict/build_bank.py`) — clusters those features per slide and writes the summarization artifacts with integrity metadata.

The training guide documents this exact command sequence: export an intermediate release, run `prepare_bank.py`, then run `build_bank.py` against its manifest [docs/training.md](/docs/training.md#L104-L115).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Intermediate release<br/>stage1 + gene_space] --> B["prepare_bank.py<br/>encode references"]
    B --> C["manifest.json<br/>E / Y / panel per object"]
    C --> D["build_bank.py<br/>PCA + k-means + summarize"]
    D --> E["Bank directory<br/>model.json + summaries/*"]
    E --> F["Final release packaging<br/>+ fusion weights"]
    F --> G["Inference: retrieval + fusion"]
```

Sources: [docs/training.md](/docs/training.md#L104-L115), [predict/build_bank.py](/predict/build_bank.py#L1-L8), [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L1-L2), [morph2mol/bank_builder.py](/morph2mol/bank_builder.py#L1)

## Stage 1: Preparing Reference Inputs with `prepare_bank.py`

`prepare_bank.py` takes a release, a prepared dataset, and a list of reference sample IDs, and emits one working directory per reference containing the bank builder's raw inputs. Its first act is a data-contract guard: the reference list must be a subset of the corpus's training split (`set(refs) <= set(contract['training_set'])`), preventing held-out slides from leaking into the retrieval pool [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L29-L30). This guard connects directly to the split discipline described in [Training Data Contracts](13-training-data-contracts); here we focus only on what construction itself produces.

The release is opened with `retrieval=False` because bank/gate artifacts do not exist yet — only the Stage-1 checkpoint and gene space are needed [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L26-L28). The gene space is loaded into a symbol→global-index lookup that anchors every later panel mapping [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L27-L28).

Sources: [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L26-L30), [docs/training.md](/docs/training.md#L104-L112)

### Mapping the slide's measured panel into the global gene space

Each reference slide measures its own subset of genes, recorded in its `genes.tsv`. The preparer intersects those symbols with the release gene space, keeping column order, rejecting slides with no overlap or duplicate measured symbols, and writing the matched symbols to `genes.txt` [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L34-L39). This per-slide "panel" is central to the whole design: the bank stores expression only for genes the slide actually measured, and retrieval later forms *coverage groups* by intersecting query panels with bank panels — mechanics detailed in [Cluster Retrieval Mechanics](11-cluster-retrieval-mechanics).

Sources: [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L34-L39)

### Encoding reference slides through the full prediction pipeline

To obtain image features, the preparer invokes the complete prediction pipeline on the reference slide itself — segmentation, crop extraction, encoding — via `predict_reference([... '--save-embeddings' ...], reference=True)`, cached as `direct.h5ad` [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L40-L45). Two validations protect the cache: the H5AD must be marked `complete`, and its recorded `stage1_sha256` must equal the current release's Stage-1 hash, otherwise stale predictions are rejected [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L52-L53). The Stage-1 Phase-1 features are then exported as `E.npy` — the `[N, 1536]` retrieval embedding matrix, with cell IDs retained to align expression rows later [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L54-L55).

Sources: [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L40-L55)

### Standardizing measured expression

Expression handling follows an explicit recipe, stated in a code comment as: *"population z-score log1p counts, sd floor 1e-3, fp16 before cluster means"* [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L57). Concretely, the sparse `expression.npz` is restricted to the predicted cell rows and matched gene columns, log1p-transformed, z-scored per gene with a variance floor of `1e-3` guarding near-constant genes, and written as a float16 memmap `Y.npy` in 4096-row chunks [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L56-L65). The per-slide panel is saved as global gene indices in `panel.npy` [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L66).

Sources: [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L56-L66)

### Provenance metadata and the manifest

Each working directory ends with a `feature_meta.json` declaring the Stage-1 checkpoint hash, the feature protocol ID (`masked_cell_features`), dimensionality 1536, and `output_field: 'phase1'` [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L67-L68). Finally the top-level `manifest.json` records the checkpoint path, gene-space path, both protocol IDs, and one object entry per reference (`split: 'train'`, `n_cells`, and `E`/`Y`/`panel` paths) [train/prepare_bank.py](/train/prepare_bank.py#L69-L73).

| Output | Content | Purpose downstream |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `E.npy` | `[N, 1536]` raw Phase-1 image features | PCA + k-means clustering keys |
| `Y.npy` | `[N, len(panel)]` float16 z-scored log1p expression | Cluster mean expression values |
| `panel.npy` | Global gene indices of the measured panel | Coverage-group formation at retrieval |
| `feature_meta.json` | Checkpoint hash + protocol IDs + dim + field | Feature provenance validation |
