# Nuclei Segmentation with Cellpose-SAM



This page explains how Morph2Mol turns a whole-slide H&E image into per-nucleus boundaries — the first, and most quality-sensitive, step of every image-based inference run. It covers the standalone CLI `predict/segment.py`, the slide-reading layer beneath it, the seam-handling rule that guarantees each nucleus is segmented exactly once, the `cells.npz` output contract, and how the segmentation is spawned automatically and consumed by the prediction pipeline. Segmentation is the only stage of inference that does not involve the Morph2Mol model itself: it delegates entirely to Cellpose-SAM (`cpsam`), an off-the-shelf segmentation foundation model.

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L1-L27), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L14-L16)

## Why Segmentation Sits at the Front of the Pipeline

Every downstream computation in Morph2Mol is anchored to a cell boundary. The per-cell image feature is a **mask-weighted average over the encoder's patch tokens**, so the polygon boundary decides which image evidence is attributed to this cell rather than to its neighbour. A slightly wrong boundary shifts the 16×16 token weighting in `predict/geometry.py`, which directly perturbs the encoder input. This is why the module documentation explicitly recommends substituting your own boundaries — for example from a pipeline paired with a spatial assay — when they exist.

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L25-L27), [geometry.py](predict/geometry.py#L19-L33)

There are two entry paths into segmentation. You can run `predict/segment.py` standalone to produce a reusable `cells.npz`, or you can omit `--cells` when calling `predict/predict.py`, in which case the prediction driver spawns `segment.py` as a subprocess and saves the result next to the prediction output. The module-interaction diagram below shows both paths; it is worth reading before the detailed sections because it names every component this page discusses.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SI["SlideReader<br/>predict/slide_io.py"] --> SEG["segment.py<br/>windowed Cellpose-SAM"]
    PRED["predict.py<br/>main driver"] -- "spawns subprocess when<br/>--image given without --cells" --> SEG
    SEG -- "writes" --> NPZ[("cells.npz")]
    NPZ -- "centroids + polygons" --> WS["WSISlide<br/>predict/inputs.py"]
    GEO["crop_px_for / polygon_mask<br/>predict/geometry.py"] --> WS
    WS --> ENC["Encoder → SE(2) decoder<br/>(model pages)"]
```

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L52-L71), [inputs.py](predict/inputs.py#L9-L14), [geometry.py](predict/geometry.py#L1-L9)

## Reading Slides: The SlideReader Backend Chain

`SlideReader` in `predict/slide_io.py` is the only component that touches image bytes. It tries three readers in order — **OpenSlide** (SVS, NDPI, MRXS, pyramidal TIFF), **tifffile** (OME-TIFF and plain TIFF), then **Pillow** (PNG, JPEG, small TIFFs). Each import is lazy, so a user who only processes PNGs never needs the OpenSlide C library installed, while a user with an SVS file gets an error message naming the missing package rather than an opaque decode failure. The backend that won is reported on the class as `backend` and echoed in the segmentation log line.

Sources: [slide_io.py](predict/slide_io.py#L1-L11), [slide_io.py](predict/slide_io.py#L27-L43)

Two `SlideReader` behaviours matter for segmentation. First, `region()` extracts an arbitrary rectangular window and **zero-pads wherever the window leaves the image**, which lets the tiling loop request windows that straddle slide edges without special-casing. Second, `_guess_mpp_openslide()` recovers physical resolution from slide properties in priority order: `openslide.mpp-x`, then `aperio.MPP`, then `tiff.XResolution` (inverted as `10000/f`). If none is present, resolution stays `None` and the caller must supply `--mpp` — there is no silent fallback, because physical scale is load-bearing for both segmentation and cropping.

Sources: [slide_io.py](predict/slide_io.py#L64-L88), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L117-L120)

## Loading the Cellpose-SAM Model

`load_model()` requires `cellpose>=4.0` (checked with a friendly install hint via `_require`) and constructs a `models.CellposeModel`. The weights resolve in one of two ways: a local checkpoint passed via `--model` (validated to exist, expanded to an absolute path), or — by default — the official `cpsam` checkpoint downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub repository `mouseland/cellpose-sam` through `hf_hub_download`. `--cpu` flips the `gpu` flag for machines without CUDA.

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L41-L58), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L100-L101), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L114)

## Channel Selection and Scale Normalization

Cellpose-SAM does not run on the full RGB image. `segment_window()` reduces each window to a **single channel before inference**: channel index 3 (the blue channel) by default, because in H&E staining the haematoxylin signal — which marks nuclei — lives in blue. The `--channel` flag is 1-based and validated to be 1, 2, or 3; greyscale input skips the extraction entirely. Flow-threshold parameters are passed straight through to `model.eval()`: `niter=250`, `flow_threshold=0.4`, `cellprob_threshold=0.0` by default.

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L61-L66), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L110-L113)

Cellpose has a trained-in prior for nucleus diameter, and scanners disagree about microns-per-pixel. The script therefore normalizes scale with a reference constant: `MPP_REF = 0.2125`, the resolution at which Cellpose's nucleus-diameter prior is quoted. Each window's scale factor is `mpp / MPP_REF` — greater than 1 means the slide is coarser than the reference, so the window is **upsampled** with PIL bilinear resizing (floored at 32 px per side) before inference. After segmentation, `inv_x`/`inv_y` inverse factors map every centroid and polygon vertex back to true slide pixels, and areas are corrected by `inv_x * inv_y`.

> [!TIP]
> This segmentation scale constant is deliberately decoupled from the model's crop geometry: the comment at `segment.py#L36-L37` states that the 55-µm crop contract lives in `predict/geometry.py` and is independent of `MPP_REF`. Changing one must never be assumed to affect the other.

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L36-L38), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L123-L127), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L146-L158)

## Windowed Tiling and the Centroid-Ownership Rule

A whole slide fits in neither memory nor a single forward pass, so segmentation proceeds in windows. The tiling grid is `ceil(width/window) × ceil(height/window)` with `--window` defaulting to 2048 slide pixels. Each window is cut with `2 × overlap` extra context on every side (`--overlap`, default 128 px): the context exists so nuclei near a seam are segmented with their full surroundings rather than truncated at the window edge. Purely black windows (`rgb.max() == 0`) are skipped as a cheap background filter.

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L7-L11), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L28-L29), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L131-L146)

The subtle part is **deduplication at seams**. Because windows overlap, a nucleus near a seam appears in two or more segmentations. The rule is: a nucleus is kept only if its centroid lies inside the window's *non-overlapping interior* — the check `x0 <= gx < x0 + tile_width and y0 <= gy < y0 + tile_height`, where `tile_width`/`tile_height` are clamped at slide edges. Since interiors partition the slide, every nucleus is assigned to **exactly one** window: straddling nuclei are neither duplicated nor dropped, and the owning window's overlap context guarantees the segmenting pass saw them whole. A second bounds check discards anything mapping outside the slide entirely.

> [!TIP]
> The overlap is what makes the centroid rule sound — it is not just a safety margin. The docstring notes the window whose interior contains the centroid also contains enough context around the nucleus to segment it properly, which is precisely what the overlap is for; `--overlap` must comfortably exceed one nucleus diameter, and the script warns at run time if it drops below 64 px.

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L107-L109), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L155-L166)

The per-window processing sequence, as executed by the main loop, is:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Cut window at (x0, y0)<br/>size W+2×ov, zero-padded at edges"] --> B{"Window all black?"}
    B -- "yes" --> Z["Skip"]
    B -- "no" --> C["Bilinear rescale<br/>by scale = mpp / 0.2125"]
    C --> D["Extract haematoxylin channel<br/>and run cpsam model.eval"]
    D --> E["Label image → centroids,<br/>areas, contours"]
    E --> F{"Centroid inside the<br/>window's own interior?"}
    F -- "yes" --> G["Inverse-map centroid, area,<br/>and polygon to slide pixels"]
    F -- "no" --> H["Discard<br/>(owned by another window)"]
    G --> I["Accumulate; log every<br/>20 windows"]
```

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L137-L168)

## Polygon Extraction and Size Filtering

`polygons_from_labels()` converts each label image into per-nucleus records without ever doing a full-image comparison per label — which the comment notes would be O(n × image) and would never finish on a slide. Instead, a single `scipy.ndimage.find_objects` pass yields every label's bounding box; each box is sliced, the area computed, and contours extracted with OpenCV `findContours` using `RETR_EXTERNAL` and `CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE`, keeping the largest contour per label. Labels smaller than `MIN_AREA_PX = 15` (Cellpose's `min_size`, applied in the rescaled window frame) are dropped as debris.

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L69-L95), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L38)

## The cells.npz Output Contract

The script's output contract is stated as complete in its own docstring: *"write them yourself if you already have segmentations."* This makes the file a stable interchange format — anything producing these keys slots into the pipeline without touching `segment.py`.

| Key | Shape / dtype | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `y_pixel`, `x_pixel` | [N] float32 | Centroids in **slide** pixels |
| `indptr` | [N+1] int64 | Polygon vertex offsets (CSR-style) into `vertex_*` |
| `vertex_x`, `vertex_y` | [V] float32 | Polygon vertices in slide pixels |
| `cell_id` | [N] str | Identifiers; `cell_0 … cell_{N-1}` from this script |
| `area_px` | [N] float32 | Area at full resolution (diagnostic only) |
| `mpp` | scalar float32 | Source resolution, stored so downstream code can recover it |
| `image` | str | Basename of the segmented image |

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L17-L23), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L174-L186), [formats.md](docs/formats.md#L7-L15)

Validation is strict where scale matters and lenient where it doesn't. A positive, finite `--mpp` is mandatory — resolved from the flag or slide metadata, otherwise the run aborts. If no nuclei are found at all, the script exits with a pointed hint to check `--channel` and `--mpp`. As a **post-run self-check**, it prints the median nucleus diameter derived from `area_px`; typical nuclei are 6–12 µm, and a value far from that range signals a wrong `--mpp` or `--channel` long before any model inference wastes time.

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L117-L122), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L171-L173), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L187-L191)

## CLI Reference

`predict/segment.py` arguments, all verified against the parser:

| Argument | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--image` | required | Slide to segment (any `SlideReader`-supported format) |
| `--out` | required | Destination `.npz` path (parent dirs auto-created) |
| `--model` | official `cpsam` | Local Cellpose-SAM checkpoint; omitted downloads from Hugging Face |
| `--mpp` | slide metadata | Microns per pixel; required when metadata lacks it |
| `--window` | 2048 | Window side in slide pixels |
| `--overlap` | 128 | Context margin per side; must exceed one nucleus diameter |
| `--channel` | 3 | 1-based RGB channel; 3 = blue = haematoxylin in H&E |
| `--niter` | 250 | Cellpose flow-iteration count |
| `--flow_threshold` | 0.4 | Cellpose flow threshold |
| `--cellprob_threshold` | 0.0 | Cellpose cell-probability threshold |
| `--cpu` | off | Force CPU inference |

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L98-L115)

The prediction driver exposes a passthrough subset — `--segment-window`, `--segment-overlap`, `--segment-model` — and constructs the segmentation output path as `<output-stem>.cells.npz` beside the prediction. It refuses to overwrite an existing segmentation file unless `--overwrite` is given, protecting you from silently re-segmenting a slide you already curated.

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L28-L33), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L52-L71)

## Choosing Between Automatic and Supplied Boundaries

Because the boundary quality bounds prediction quality, the pipeline offers three input modes. The comparison below reflects documented behaviour only:

| Mode | Mechanism | Boundaries | When to use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Automatic | `--image` without `--cells` | Cellpose-SAM nuclei, generated on the fly and saved to `cells.npz` | No measured segmentation available |
| Supplied | `--image` + `--cells cells.npz` | Your own polygons in source-image pixels (same contract) | Boundaries exist from your pipeline or a paired spatial assay |
| Prepared | `--prepared slide_dir` | Pre-cut crops with `patch_cell_boundaries.npz` | Training/benchmark layout; skips live slide access entirely |

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L13-L16), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L43-L44), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L25-L27), [README.md](README.md#L68-L80)

## Downstream Consumption of cells.npz

`WSISlide` in `predict/inputs.py` is the consumer. It loads `y_pixel`/`x_pixel` into a position array, optionally the polygon triplet (`indptr`, `vertex_x`, `vertex_y`) — absent polygons degrade gracefully to a centre-token mask rather than an error — and `cell_id` with a positional fallback naming scheme. Its resolution recovery is a three-step fallback chain, checked in order:

| Priority | Source of mpp | Mechanism |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | CLI `--mpp` | Passed explicitly to `WSISlide(image, cells, mpp)` |
| 2 | Slide metadata | Fresh `SlideReader` probe (`openslide.mpp-x`, `aperio.MPP`, `tiff.XResolution`) |
| 3 | `cells.npz` `mpp` scalar | Stored by `segment.py` at write time |

Sources: [inputs.py](predict/inputs.py#L14-L33)

From the resolved `mpp`, `WSISlide` computes the crop side via `crop_px_for()` — `55 µm / mpp`, the physical field-of-view contract every training slide shares — and batches cell-centred crops resized to the encoder's 224 px input. Polygon vertices are translated into crop-local coordinates, scaled from slide pixels to the crop frame, and rasterized by `polygon_mask()` into a normalized **16×16 token mask** that mirrors the training-time construction exactly; degenerate polygons fall back to the centre token so no cell yields a zero-weight feature.

Sources: [inputs.py](predict/inputs.py#L49-L64), [geometry.py](predict/geometry.py#L6-L16), [geometry.py](predict/geometry.py#L19-L33)

Note that `SlideReader` handles are opened per worker inside `WSISlide` because slide handles are not fork-safe — a detail that matters if you embed this class in your own multiprocessing code.

Sources: [inputs.py](predict/inputs.py#L43-L47)

## Troubleshooting

Symptoms map to a small set of root causes, all checkable before model inference:

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Physical resolution is required` at start | Metadata lacks mpp and no `--mpp` | Pass `--mpp` in µm/pixel |
| `no nuclei found` after all windows | Wrong channel or absurd scale | Check `--channel` (3 = blue for H&E) and `--mpp` |
| Median diameter far outside 6–12 µm | Wrong `--mpp` or `--channel` | Use the post-run diagnostic to recalibrate inputs |
| Nuclei cut at seams in results | `--overlap` too small | Increase overlap; warning fires below 64 px |
| Missing SVS/NDPI support | OpenSlide not installed | Install `openslide-python` + the OpenSlide C library |
| Prediction run refuses to start: `cells.npz exists` | Prior segmentation beside output | Pass it via `--cells`, or rerun with `--overwrite` |

Sources: [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L117-L127), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L171-L173), [segment.py](predict/segment.py#L186-L191), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L60-L62), [slide_io.py](predict/slide_io.py#L46-L62)

## Where to Go Next

Segmentation output feeds directly into spatial processing: [Spatial Context Blocking](19-spatial-context-blocking) explains how the centroids and cell ordering produced here organize cells into attention blocks, and [Streaming Output and Fault Tolerance](20-streaming-output-and-fault-tolerance) covers how per-cell results reach disk without holding a slide's worth of predictions in memory. For the command-line surface surrounding this workflow, see [Inference CLI Reference](3-inference-cli-reference); for interpreting what lands in the `.h5ad` after segmentation-driven inference, see [Reading Prediction Outputs](4-reading-prediction-outputs). The architecture behind the mask-weighted features that boundaries control is detailed in [Image Encoder and LoRA Adapters](6-image-encoder-and-lora-adapters).

# Spatial Context Blocking



Spatial context blocking is the inference-side mechanism that turns a whole-slide cell list into a deterministic stream of **target/context blocks**: each block owns up to 128 target cells whose predictions are committed exactly once, plus up to 64 surrounding context cells that sharpen the SE(2) distance-attention decode but are never written. The blocking module, `predict/spatial_context.py`, deliberately reuses the *exact* partition and halo kernels that Stage-2 training used, so that every inference batch reproduces the spatial statistics the decoder was trained on — with no expression values read at inference time. This page dissects the planning objects, the partition kernel, halo assembly, and the streaming/commit loop that consumes blocks.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Inputs
        SEG["cells.npz from segmentation"] --> SRC["predict/inputs.py<br/>WSISlide or PreparedSlide"]
    end
    subgraph Planning
        REC["morph2mol/recipe.py<br/>128 targets, 64 context, 137 um"] --> PLAN["predict/spatial_context.py<br/>TargetContextPlan"]
        KER["morph2mol/full_coverage.py<br/>partition_cells + halo_cells"] --> PLAN
        PLAN -->|"order, ptr, kdtree"| DS["TargetContextDataset"]
    end
    SRC -->|"batch indices: crops + token masks"| DS
    DS -->|"images, masks, indices, n_targets"| LOOP["predict/predict.py<br/>streaming loop"]
    LOOP -->|"encode + decode, SE(2) attention over block"| PAY["commit_target_rows"]
    PAY --> H5[("streamed .h5ad<br/>layers A / X, obsm, uns")]
```

## Why Blocks Exist: Training-Matched Spatial Batching

The SE(2) expression decoder consumes a *set* of cells with micron coordinates, not a single crop: predictions for target cells are conditioned on neighbors within a spatial radius. At training time, Stage 2 batches "up to 128 supervised cells and 64 additional context cells" per step with a maximum decoder distance of 137 µm, and context cells attend but never enter the loss. Inference must reproduce this receptive field exactly — a cell predicted in isolation would see an attention neighborhood the decoder never encountered. Blocking therefore serves three simultaneous purposes: **training-matched batching** (identical target/context composition), **bounded memory** (each block is at most 192 crops of 55 µm, streamed one at a time through a `batch_size=None` DataLoader), and **exactly-once output ownership** (partitioned ownership lets the streaming HDF5 writer scatter rows without collisions). The module docstring states the invariant plainly: reuse the actual training partition/halo functions; commit only the target prefix, once per cell.

Sources: [spatial_context.py](predict/spatial_context.py#L1-L5), [stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L186-L196), [training.md](docs/training.md#L62-L95), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L135-L136)

## Block Anatomy and Recipe Constants

Every numeric constant in the block contract comes from the frozen Morph2Mol-25M recipe, shared verbatim by training and inference. The recipe module raises if any runtime argument attempts to override these values, so the geometry below is a hard contract, not a default.

| Constant | Value | Role in blocking |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TARGET_CELLS` | 128 | Maximum owned targets per block |
| `CONTEXT_CELLS` | 64 | Maximum halo cells appended after targets |
| `RADIUS_UM` | 137.0 | Context query radius (≈2.5 × the 55 µm crop side) |
| `SEED` | 1 | Base seed; per-slide seed derives from `crc32` of the object name |
| `FOV_UM` (geometry) | 55.0 | Physical crop side every cell image covers |
| Partition epoch | 0 (frozen) | Training rotates the partition per epoch; inference pins epoch 0 |

A block is therefore a flat index array `[targets, context]` of length ≤ 192, paired with the integer `n_targets` that marks the ownership boundary. The 55 µm crop field of view and the 137 µm halo radius are dimensionally compatible by design: context cells are typically the immediate ring of neighbors whose own crops overlap the target's surroundings.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    B["One inference block: up to 128 + 64 = 192 rows"] --> T["Target prefix, owned cells<br/>predictions scattered to output matrices"]
    B --> C["Halo suffix, context cells<br/>attend in the decoder, never written"]
    T -->|"halo_cells: nearest neighbours within 137 um,<br/>deduplicated and capped at 64"| C
```

Sources: [recipe.py](morph2mol/recipe.py#L4-L8), [geometry.py](predict/geometry.py#L6-L9), [spatial_context.py](predict/spatial_context.py#L20-L27)

## TargetContextPlan: Deterministic Ownership Planning

`TargetContextPlan` is constructed once per run from the slide's micron positions — derived as source pixels × mpp in `covariates.geometry` — and the sample identity, which defaults to the input file stem (`--sample-id` overrides it). Determinism is anchored in a content-derived seed: `object_seed = (SEED + zlib.crc32(object_name)) % (2**31 - 1)`, so the *same sample id always yields the same partition*, while different slides get independent, decorrelated block layouts. The plan computes the ownership ordering eagerly via `partition_cells` and builds its `cKDTree` lazily on the first halo query; iteration then reduces to slicing contiguous ranges from the `order` array through the `ptr` offset table.

```python
self.object_seed = (SEED + zlib.crc32(self.object_name.encode())) % (2**31 - 1)
self.order, self.ptr = partition_cells(self.pos, self.target_cells, self.object_seed, self.epoch)
```

> [!TIP]
> Because `object_seed` hashes the *name* rather than the coordinates, renaming the input file (or changing `--sample-id`) changes the partition entirely — still valid and still exactly-once, but block boundaries will differ. Downstream consumers comparing block-level logs across runs should pin `--sample-id`.

Sources: [spatial_context.py](predict/spatial_context.py#L15-L40), [covariates.py](predict/covariates.py#L22-L37), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L107-L108)

## The Partition Kernel: `partition_cells`

The shared kernel in `morph2mol/full_coverage.py` converts N unordered cell positions into a flattened, non-overlapping ownership sequence in five deterministic steps, all driven by the seeded RNG:

1. **Seeded rotation** — the grid axis is rotated by an angle uniform in `[-π/4, π/4)` derived from `(seed + epoch*1000003) % (2**31-1)`, decorrelating partitions across epochs.
2. **Raster grid with 2× sizing** — the grid cell side is `sqrt(span_x·span_y·target_cells·2/N)`, i.e. sized to hold roughly *twice* the target budget on average.
3. **Jittered origin** — the grid origin is offset by a random fraction of one cell side, preventing systematic alignment artifacts with tissue structure.
4. **Median bisection** — each raster cell holding more than 128 points is recursively split along its widest axis at the median (ties broken by original index), so every emitted block satisfies the target budget.
5. **Ownership proof** — a `bincount` assertion verifies every cell appears exactly once in the flattened output before `order`/`ptr` are returned.

> [!TIP]
> The 2× grid-sizing factor means nearly every raster cell bisects into two ~128-cell blocks, blending the cache-friendly locality of raster blocking with the budget guarantee of kd-splitting. Blocks are emitted in rotated-grid raster order, and within a block targets are sorted along the split axis — spatially coherent, fully deterministic.

Sources: [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L14-L40)

## Halo Assembly: `halo_cells`

For each block, context is assembled by a bounded nearest-neighbor query over the plan's k-d tree. The algorithm exploits an ordering invariant rather than a heap or set:

1. Query the `k = min(16, N)` nearest neighbors of every target — at most 128 × 16 = 2048 candidate entries.
2. Mask candidates to those within `RADIUS_UM` = 137 µm that are **not** owned targets of this block.
3. Reshape the mask to *neighbor-rank-major* order (`ids.T[valid.T]`), so candidates appear rank-0 neighbors of all targets first, then rank-1, and so on.
4. `np.unique(..., return_index=True)` keeps each distinct context cell at its **first occurrence** — which, given the rank-major ordering, is its closest announcing target.
5. `np.sort(first)` restores rank-major order among survivors, and `[:context_cells]` truncates to the 64-cell cap.

The result is a halo that prioritizes globally nearest cells with fully deterministic ordering — with one edge case: when a single block owns the entire slide, there are no *outside* cells and the halo is legitimately empty. The same kernel serves training's `FullCoverageDataset`, where the halo additionally feeds a boolean `mask` (`arange(len(idx)) < n_targets`) separating supervised rows from context rows.

Sources: [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L43-L52), [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L113-L127)

## Streaming Blocks Through the Prediction Loop

`TargetContextDataset` is a thin adapter: for block `b` it asks the plan for `indices` and `n_targets`, calls `source.batch(indices)` to cut 55 µm crops and rasterize cell polygons into normalized 16×16 token masks, and returns tensors. The prediction loop consumes it with `DataLoader(batch_size=None)` — each `__getitem__` yields one complete block, distributed across CPU workers (slide handles are opened per worker because they are not fork-safe). Per block, the loop encodes all 192 images with the Stage-2 LoRA adapters, decodes with micron coordinates and area covariates for **targets and context alike** (the SE(2) attention needs the full neighborhood), then commits only the owned prefix:

| Payload tensor | Committed rows | Condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `A` (direct expression, `layers/A`) | owned prefix only | always |
| `X` (final matrix in reference mode) | owned prefix only | `reference=True` calibration |
| `H2` stage-2 features, `Z` SE(2) features (`obsm`) | owned prefix only | `--save-embeddings` |
| `H1` phase-1 features (`obsm`) | owned prefix only | encoded separately from `images[:n_targets]` — context never re-encoded |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P["pos_um micron coordinates<br/>from covariates.geometry"] --> A["partition_cells<br/>seeded rotation, raster grid, median bisection"]
    A --> O["order + ptr<br/>every cell owned exactly once"]
    O --> H["halo_cells<br/>k nearest within 137 um, dedup, cap 64"]
    H --> I["indices = targets, then context"]
    I --> L["source.batch<br/>55 um crops + 16x16 token masks"]
    L --> M["encode + decode over the full block"]
    M --> W["commit_target_rows<br/>scatter owned prefix only"]
    W --> F["written counter == 1 for every cell"]
```

Sources: [spatial_context.py](predict/spatial_context.py#L50-L61), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L135-L157), [inputs.py](predict/inputs.py#L46-L62)

## Exactly-Once Commit and Integrity Guards

`commit_target_rows` is the serialization gate between the GPU and the streamed HDF5 file. It validates the ownership prefix before any scatter: `n_targets` must be in `(0, len(indices)]`, the owned ids must be unique, and the write-counter must still be zero for every one of them. Each payload is then scattered in sorted-id order (a deterministic write order independent of within-block target ordering), and the counter increments. The loop finishes with a global assertion that `written == 1` for all N cells — the full-coverage guarantee that no cell was silently dropped by a worker failure or an off-by-one in partitioning.

| Guard | Trigger | Raised error |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Position shape | non-empty `[cells, 2]` required in plan init | `ValueError: Expected nonempty [cells, 2] micron positions` |
| Partition validity | any cell owned ≠ once after `partition_cells` | `ValueError: Spatial partition must own every target exactly once` |
| Prefix sanity | `n_targets` outside `(0, len(indices)]` | `ValueError: Invalid owned target prefix` |
| Duplicate write | owned ids repeat or counter already nonzero | `ValueError: A target cell would be written more than once` |
| Payload width | model output shorter than the block | `ValueError: Model output does not cover the complete target/context batch` |
| Numeric sanity | nonfinite direct prediction | `RuntimeError: Nonfinite direct prediction` |
| Final coverage | any cell with `written != 1` after the loop | `RuntimeError: Prediction must write each target cell exactly once` |

Sources: [spatial_context.py](predict/spatial_context.py#L64-L78), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L144-L161)

## Provenance Metadata and the Calibration Protocol

Every block plan exposes a `metadata()` dict that is committed verbatim into the output file at `uns['morph2mol']['spatial_context']`: the partition `revision` (`full_coverage_halo_v1`), target/context budgets, context radius, base seed, the hashed object seed, partition object and epoch, block count, and the two policy flags `output_policy='targets_once_only'` and `partition_fixed_for_inference=True`. This makes any output file self-describing with respect to *how* its cells were blocked. Alongside it, `prediction_protocol()` returns the canonical protocol values, and `check_prediction_protocol(metadata)` rejects any metadata that diverges from the deployed settings — the handshake ensuring that fusion-gate calibration and spatial prediction were computed under identical blocking rules.

Sources: [spatial_context.py](predict/spatial_context.py#L42-L47), [spatial_context.py](predict/spatial_context.py#L81-L90), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L116-L117), [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L11)

## Training and Inference: One Kernel, Two Schedules

The deepest design decision in this page is that inference imports the *training* kernel rather than reimplementing it. Stage 2 wraps the same `partition_cells`/`halo_cells` in `CoveragePlan`, which generates an epoch-specific partition per slide, shuffles block order across ranks, and caches partitions on disk; inference pins epoch 0, iterates blocks sequentially, and recomputes the plan in-process (slides are far smaller than training corpora). Both sides rely on `supervised_sums`-style masking — in training via a boolean mask that keeps context out of the negative-binomial and MSE losses, in inference via the `n_targets` prefix that keeps context out of the output writer.

| Dimension | Stage-2 training (`CoveragePlan`) | Inference (`TargetContextPlan`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kernel functions | `partition_cells` + `halo_cells` | identical imports |
| Epoch schedule | new seeded partition per epoch (3 epochs) | fixed `epoch=0` |
| Block order | per-rank stride + seeded permutation | sequential, raster order |
| Context role | SE(2) attention; masked out of both losses | SE(2) attention; never committed to outputs |
| Coverage contract | every usable target once *per epoch* | every target once *per run* |
| Partition reuse | `cached_arrays` disk cache with signature stamps | recomputed in memory |
| Failure semantics | mask zeroed for invalid slots (padding) | hard errors on any coverage violation |

This table explains why a released model can be pointed at arbitrary new tissue: the decoder's neighborhood statistics at inference are drawn from the same distribution of block compositions it was optimized under.

Sources: [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L55-L105), [full_coverage.py](morph2mol/full_coverage.py#L130-L139), [stage2.py](morph2mol/training/stage2.py#L133-L139), [docs](docs/training.md#L62-L95)

## Where to Go Next

To see what the context cells actually *do* inside the decoder, continue to [SE(2) Distance Attention Decoder](7-se-2-distance-attention-decoder) and [Negative-Binomial Expression Head](8-negative-binomial-expression-head); for the training-side schedule these blocks replicate, read [Stage 2 Expression Training](15-stage-2-expression-training). The commit guards interact directly with the streamed writer covered in [Streaming Output and Fault Tolerance](20-streaming-output-and-fault-tolerance), and the `spatial_context` block embedded in `uns` is one of the fields to inspect in [Reading Prediction Outputs](4-reading-prediction-outputs). Upstream, the micron positions consumed by `TargetContextPlan` originate from [Nuclei Segmentation with Cellpose-SAM](18-nuclei-segmentation-with-cellpose-sam), and the `--sample-id` flag that seeds the partition is documented in the [Inference CLI Reference](3-inference-cli-reference).

# Streaming Output and Fault Tolerance



A whole-slide inference run can involve hundreds of thousands of cells and millions of gene values — far more than you want to hold in RAM, and far too expensive to lose to a crash at minute 90. This page explains how Morph2Mol's inference CLI (`predict/predict.py`) solves both problems with a single design: results are **streamed into a pre-allocated, chunked HDF5 staging file** under strict *exactly-once* write discipline, and the final result is **published atomically** only after every invariant has passed. We walk through the write pipeline, the once-only commit protocol, the fail-fast guards, the I/O fallback chain, and the resource lifecycle — everything that lets a long-running prediction fail loudly and cheaply, or succeed cleanly.

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L19), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L145-L168)

## The Staged Write Pipeline

The `--out` argument is documented as "Output .h5ad; matrices are streamed to disk", and the implementation backs that promise with a two-phase commit. The CLI immediately resolves the output path and derives a sibling staging path — `results.h5ad` becomes `results.h5ad.partial` — and refuses to start if either file already exists unless you pass `--overwrite`. All writes during the run go to the `.partial` file; the real output path is never touched by an incomplete run.

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L19), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L45-L49)

Inside the staging file, every result matrix is **pre-allocated before any GPU work begins**. A `matrix()` helper creates fixed-shape HDF5 datasets with explicit chunking (`chunks=(min(n,128), min(shape[1],512))`) and lossless `lzf` compression, so a 300,000-cell × 5,000-gene `layers/A` never exists in memory as one array — it lives on disk in ~128×512 tiles. The datasets created up front are `layers/A` (the direct NB-head predictions), `X` (the fused output), `obsm/X_morph2mol_phase1` (retrieval keys, float16 to halve I/O), and optionally the stage-2/SE(2) embeddings when `--save-embeddings` is set. During the encoding loop, each target/context block is processed, validated, and scattered into these pre-allocated arrays row-group by row-group; nothing accumulates.

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L126-L141), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L144-L159)

The full lifecycle is one directed pipeline with a single publication gate:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["CLI start<br/>validate args, resolve out + .partial"] --> B["Segmentation subprocess<br/>check=True, writes cells.npz"]
    B --> C["Open .partial HDF5<br/>attrs complete=False"]
    C --> D["Pre-allocate chunked datasets<br/>A, X, H1 (+H2, Z)"]
    D --> E["Encoding loop per block<br/>encode → decode → finite check"]
    E --> F{"np.isfinite<br/>all values?"}
    F -- "no" --> X1["RuntimeError, abort"]
    F -- "yes" --> G["commit_target_rows<br/>scatter target rows, count += 1"]
    G --> H{"more blocks?"}
    H -- "yes" --> E
    H -- "no" --> I{"written == 1<br/>for every cell?"}
    I -- "no" --> X2["RuntimeError, abort"]
    I -- "yes" --> J["Tear down model/GPU memory"]
    J --> K["Retrieval + fusion pass<br/>stream R and X per query batch"]
    K --> L["Set complete=True, flush"]
    L --> M["os.replace(partial → out)<br/>atomic publication"]
```

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L126-L168), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L169-L201)

## The Exactly-Once Row Commit Protocol

Streaming writes are only safe if every cell lands in the output **exactly once** — and the block structure makes that nontrivial, because each block carries *target* cells (owned, must be written) plus *halo context* cells (borrowed for the decoder, must never be written). The commit function `commit_target_rows` in `morph2mol/spatial_context.py` encodes this contract. It takes the block's index array and the `n_targets` prefix length, and enforces three guards in order: the target prefix must be non-empty and well-formed, the owned indices must be unique *and* never previously written (`counts[owned] == 0` before the scatter), and every model payload must cover the full batch — a shorter prediction array than the block's index list is a hard error rather than a silent partial write. Only after all scatters succeed does it increment the per-cell write counters.

Sources: [morph2mol/spatial_context.py](morph2mol/spatial_context.py#L64-L78), [morph2mol/spatial_context.py](morph2mol/spatial_context.py#L42-L47)

The main loop complements this with an end-of-run audit. A `uint8` counter array of length *n* is allocated alongside the loader, incremented by each successful commit, and finally checked with `np.all(written == 1)` — if any cell was written zero times or more than once, the run aborts instead of publishing a silently incomplete `.h5ad`. This is defense in depth: the per-commit guard catches a bad block immediately, and the global audit catches any gap the per-block checks could miss (for example, a partition that fails to cover the slide).

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L142-L144), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L159), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L167-L168)

> [!TIP]
> The same `commit_target_rows` function is shared by reference calibration and deployed inference (`prediction_protocol()` pins `output_policy='targets_once_only'`), so the once-only guarantee is a *protocol*, not a per-script convention — metadata written into `uns/morph2mol.spatial_context` lets any consumer verify it.

Sources: [morph2mol/spatial_context.py](morph2mol/spatial_context.py#L42-L47), [morph2mol/spatial_context.py](morph2mol/spatial_context.py#L81-L91)

## Atomic Publication and the Completion Flag

Three mechanisms cooperate so that a reader can never observe a half-written result. First, the staging file opens with the attribute `complete=False`, which is flipped to `True` only after all post-processing (fusion metadata, `beta`/`covered` gene flags, spatial coordinates, provenance `uns`) has been written and flushed. Second, the file itself is renamed into place with `os.replace(partial, out)` — an atomic filesystem operation on POSIX systems, so the output path transitions from *absent* to *fully valid* in one step. Third, the startup guard rejects a run when either the output or a stale `.partial` exists, preventing a new run from silently mixing its rows into someone else's leftover file.

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L126-L127), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L192-L200), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L45-L49)

The most expensive preprocessing stage gets its own durability story. Automatic segmentation runs as a **separate subprocess** launched with `subprocess.run(..., check=True)`, writing a self-contained `cells.npz` (centroids, polygon vertices, cell IDs) next to the eventual output. Two consequences follow: if segmentation crashes, the Python process aborts *before* creating any output files (no orphaned GPU state, no partial HDF5); and because the `.cells.npz` survives a crashed or completed run, you can restart cheaply by passing it explicitly via `--cells`, skipping re-segmentation entirely.

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L52-L71), [predict/segment.py](predict/segment.py#L17-L23)

## Fail-Fast Validation and Runtime Guards

The design philosophy is to **fail before the expensive work begins, and loudly the moment invariants break**. Argument validation runs first — microns-per-pixel must be a positive physical scale, batch sizes and worker counts must be sane, `--cells` is rejected with `--prepared` — followed by data-level checks the moment inputs are opened: empty inputs, duplicate cell identifiers, and gene panels that are empty, duplicated, or absent from the model's gene head all raise before the model loads. Then, *during* the GPU loop, each block's decoded predictions are checked with `np.isfinite(...).all()`, so a numerical blow-up kills the run at the offending block instead of poisoning thousands of rows downstream.

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L39-L48), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L86-L105), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L152-L153)

The same philosophy extends through the toolchain with actionable error messages rather than stack traces. The segmentation stage validates `--mpp`, window/overlap/channel parameters up front, warns when `--overlap` is small enough to risk cutting nuclei at window seams, and if a slide yields zero nuclei it exits with a diagnostic naming the two usual suspects (`--channel`, `--mpp`). Slides lacking physical-resolution metadata are refused with an explicit instruction to pass `--mpp`, rather than silently guessing a scale.

Sources: [predict/segment.py](predict/segment.py#L118-L128), [predict/segment.py](predict/segment.py#L172-L173), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L56-L58)

The following matrix maps each anticipated failure to its detection mechanism and the user-visible behavior:

| Failure scenario | Detection mechanism | Behavior | Recovery path |
|---|---|---|---|
| Crash mid-run (OOM, power loss) | `.partial` staging file never renamed | Output path stays clean; `complete` flag stays `False` | Fix cause, rerun; reuse `cells.npz` via `--cells` |
| Stale output/partial exists | Startup `FileExistsError` guard | Run refuses to start | Choose new path or pass `--overwrite` |
| NaN/Inf from the decoder | Per-block `np.isfinite().all()` | `RuntimeError` naming the block | Investigate input patch; abort beats silent corruption |
| Partition misses or double-hits a cell | `commit_target_rows` counters + final `written == 1` audit | `RuntimeError`; `.partial` never promoted | Library bug, not user error — report with the input |
| Missing slide resolution metadata | MPP check before model load | `ValueError` instructing `--mpp` | Supply `--mpp` in µm/pixel |
| TIFF without OpenSlide installed | Lazy backend fallback with install hints | `RuntimeError` naming `pip install tifffile` / OpenSlide | Install the suggested package |
| Segmentation finds no nuclei | `SystemExit` with hint | Process exits before prediction starts | Check `--channel` (3 = blue for H&E) and `--mpp` |
| Crop extends past slide edge | Zero-padded `region()` read | Cell kept, rows stay aligned | None needed — order always matches input |

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L39-L58), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L152-L153), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L167-L168), [predict/slide_io.py](predict/slide_io.py#L45-L62), [predict/segment.py](predict/segment.py#L172-L173), [predict/slide_io.py](predict/slide_io.py#L76-L88)

## I/O Backend Fallbacks and Worker Isolation

Reading whole-slide imagery is inherently environment-dependent, so `SlideReader` degrades gracefully rather than hard-failing. It tries **three backends in order** — OpenSlide (SVS/NDPI/MRXS/pyramidal TIFF), tifffile (OME/plain TIFF), then Pillow (PNG/JPEG) — with all imports deferred until needed, so a PNG-only user never needs OpenSlide installed and an SVS user who lacks it gets an error message naming the exact package to install instead of an opaque decode failure. When a crop extends beyond the slide boundary it is **zero-padded rather than dropped**, which preserves the invariant that output row order always matches input cell order — a quiet but essential precondition for the scatter-based commit protocol.

Sources: [predict/slide_io.py](predict/slide_io.py#L1-L11), [predict/slide_io.py](predict/slide_io.py#L16-L24), [predict/slide_io.py](predict/slide_io.py#L45-L62), [predict/slide_io.py](predict/slide_io.py#L76-L88)

Concurrency introduces its own failure class: DataLoader worker processes fork the parent, but **slide file handles are not fork-safe**. `WSISlide` therefore never opens the slide eagerly — it stores the path and opens a private `SlideReader` lazily inside each worker process on first use. Each worker owns its handle, so a worker crash or restart cannot corrupt another worker's file position, and crop loading proceeds in parallel (`--workers`) without shared mutable I/O state.

Sources: [predict/inputs.py](predict/inputs.py#L43-L47)

## Resource Reclamation Between Phases

Inference runs in two memory-heavy phases: block-wise encoding (model on GPU, image batches streaming through) followed by retrieval and gated fusion (a reference bank resident on the device, queries batched by `--query-batch`). Between the two, the pipeline **deliberately tears down everything it no longer needs** — the model and batch tensors are deleted, the parent's slide reader handle is closed, `gc.collect()` reclaims Python objects, and `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` returns GPU memory to the driver. On a large slide this is the difference between the fusion pass fitting comfortably and an out-of-memory death at the 99% mark; the final audit has already passed, so everything in the staging file at that point is valid.

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L167-L174), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L177-L188)

> [!TIP]
> Because the fusion pass reads `H1` back *from the staging file* in query batches and writes `R`/`X` rows as it goes, peak memory during fusion is `query_batch × g` — independent of slide size. If you hit GPU limits on the *encoding* phase, lower `--enc-chunk` and `--query-batch`; slide size itself does not set the memory ceiling.

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L181-L188), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L136-L141)

## How Long Jobs Stay Observable

Fault tolerance includes knowing a job is alive. Every progress printer uses `flush=True` — output is never trapped in a buffer you can't see when tailing a log over SSH or inside a container — and both phases report at fixed intervals: the segmentation subprocess prints a per-window heartbeat every 20 windows (with elapsed time and running nuclei count), the encoding loop prints `[A] blocks k/N` every 20 blocks, and the fusion pass prints `[retrieval + fusion] cells/n` per query batch. A stalled log line is therefore a genuine stall signal, not a buffering artifact.

Sources: [predict/segment.py](predict/segment.py#L167-L168), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L165-L166), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L186-L188)

## Putting It Together

The module interactions behind one streaming prediction look like this:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph CLI["predict/predict.py"]
        V["Validation +<br/>partial-path guard"] --> SEG["segment.py subprocess<br/>(check=True)"]
        SEG --> NPZ[("cells.npz")]
        NPZ --> LOOP["Block loop"]
    end
    subgraph Data["Data layer"]
        SRC["WSISlide / PreparedSlide"] -- "per-worker lazy handle" --> RD["SlideReader<br/>OpenSlide → tifffile → Pillow"]
    end
    subgraph Store["Streaming store (.partial HDF5)"]
        DS["Pre-allocated chunked datasets<br/>A, X, H1, (R), (H2, Z)"]
    end
    RD -- "zero-padded crops" --> LOOP
    LOOP -- "exactly-once scatter" --> DS
    LOOP -- "counters + isfinite" --> AUDIT["written==1 audit"]
    AUDIT -- "complete=True" --> REN["os.replace → out.h5ad"]
```

The takeaway for operators: a successful run publishes atomically and carries a machine-checkable `complete` flag; a failed run costs you at most the time since the last block, always leaves the output path untouched, and usually leaves you a reusable `cells.npz`. The takeaway for developers extending the pipeline: any new per-cell output should ride the same contract — add a payload to `commit_target_rows`, extend the `written` audit, and never write outside the `.partial` file.

Sources: [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L45-L49), [morph2mol/spatial_context.py](morph2mol/spatial_context.py#L64-L78), [predict.py](predict/predict.py#L192-L201)

## Where to Go Next

For how the block structure that the commit protocol depends on is constructed — target ownership, halo context, and the deterministic partition — continue with [Spatial Context Blocking](19-spatial-context-blocking). For how the segmentation subprocess produces the `cells.npz` you can reuse across reruns, see [Nuclei Segmentation with Cellpose-SAM](18-nuclei-segmentation-with-cellpose-sam). To interpret the datasets this pipeline streams into the final `.h5ad` (including the `complete` flag, `layers/A` vs `layers/R` vs `X`, and provenance metadata), read [Reading Prediction Outputs](4-reading-prediction-outputs), and for verifying that a downloaded release is intact before you point `--release` at it, see [Release Integrity Verification](21-release-integrity-verification).

# Release Integrity Verification



A deployed Morph2Mol release is a directory of independently produced artifacts: frozen encoder weights, a Stage-1 alignment checkpoint, a Stage-2 expression checkpoint, a gene space, and — optionally — a retrieval reference bank plus a fusion gate. This page explains the **release integrity verification** system: the mechanism that proves, at load time and without any access to the training corpus, that every artifact in a release directory belongs to the same training run, the same gene ordering, and the same calibration protocol. The design goal is that a mixed, stale, or hand-edited release cannot load silently; it fails fast with a specific error.

Sources: [release.py](/morph2mol/release.py#L1-L4)

## The Problem the System Solves

Because artifacts are produced at different points in the lifecycle (training, bank building, gate fitting, export), a release directory can fail in ways that would be invisible to a generic loader: a Stage-2 head trained against a different Stage-1 initializer, a bank whose embeddings live in another gene space, a fusion gate calibrated under an older spatial-blocking revision, or a `beta.json` edited after calibration. Morph2Mol's answer is to make every artifact *self-describing* — each checkpoint and sidecar carries SHA-256 identities of everything it depends on — and to have the loader cross-examine those identities against the bytes actually on disk.

The verification logic is deliberately concentrated in one portable class, `morph2mol.release.Release`, whose docstring states the contract: portable release paths and identities, no training corpus required at inference. Everything downstream — the inference CLI, the model constructor, the retrieval bank — either consumes the verified `Release` object or re-derives the same checks itself.

Sources: [release.py](/morph2mol/release.py#L1), [model.py](/predict/model.py#L1-L2)

## The Manifest Contract: release.json

Every release directory is anchored by a `release.json` manifest. The very first check is a **schema gate**: the manifest's `schema` field must be one of two whitelisted values (`morph2mol-release-v1` or `voice25m-release-v1`); anything else aborts with `Unsupported release.json schema`. This ensures the loader never interprets an unknown directory layout as a release. The dual schema support mirrors the dual key namespaces tolerated in prediction outputs (`morph2mol` / `voice25m`), so legacy releases remain loadable.

The manifest then declares relative paths for each artifact, and the loader resolves and **existence-checks** each one — the four mandatory artifacts (`uni2h`, `stage1`, `stage2`, `gene_space`) plus `bank` and `gate` when retrieval mode is requested. A missing artifact raises `FileNotFoundError` naming the exact path, so incomplete copies fail before any weights are touched.

Sources: [release.py](/morph2mol/release.py#L10-L20), [prediction_io.py](/morph2mol/prediction_io.py#L4-L7)

The example manifest shows the full field inventory an export produces:

| Manifest field | Points to | Role in verification |
|---|---|---|
| `schema` | — | Format whitelist; rejects foreign directories |
| `uni2h` | `uni2h/` | Frozen encoder directory; existence-checked |
| `stage1` | `stage1.pt` | Alignment LoRA tensors; hashed, bound to Stage-2 |
| `stage2` | `stage2.pt` | Expression weights; carries its own identities |
| `gene_space` | `gene_space.npz` | Gene ordering; hashed and semantically bound |
| `bank` | `bank/` | Reference bank; verified inside `ReferenceBank` |
| `gate` | `beta.json` | Fusion weights; bound via its `.meta.json` sidecar |
| `xenium_genes` | `xenium_genes.tsv` | Optional panel export; presence-conditional |
| `sha256` | — | Raw-file checksums for `stage1`, `stage2`, `gene_space` |

Sources: [release.example.json](/configs/release.example.json#L1-L11)

## The Verification Stack

Conceptually, `Release.__init__` runs six verification layers in order, each cheap enough to execute on every load and each failing with a targeted message. The first three layers guard the manifest and the files; the remaining three apply only in retrieval mode and guard the *relationships* between artifacts.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Load release.json"] --> B{"Layer 1: schema gate<br/>morph2mol-release-v1<br/>voice25m-release-v1"}
    B -->|accepted| C["Layer 2: artifact existence<br/>uni2h, stage1, stage2, gene_space<br/>(+ bank, gate if retrieval)"]
    C --> D["Layer 3: manifest SHA-256<br/>stage1 / stage2 / gene_space"]
    D --> E{"retrieval mode?"}
    E -->|no| I["Release ready<br/>(non-retrieval consumers)"]
    E -->|yes| F["Layer 4: cross-artifact<br/>binding web (7 checks)"]
    F --> G["Layer 5: spatial-context<br/>protocol pin"]
    G --> H["Layer 6: retrieval settings<br/>K and tau consistency"]
    H --> I
```

Layers 1–3 run for every consumer; notably, gate fitting itself instantiates `Release(retrieval=False)` precisely to reuse layers 1–3 while the bank and gate are still being *produced*. Layers 4–6 run for deployment, where all artifact families must cohere.

Sources: [release.py](/morph2mol/release.py#L7-L26), [fit_beta.py](/train/fit_beta.py#L28)

## The Cross-Artifact Binding Web

The core of the system is a **binding web**: seven pairwise identity comparisons that tie the four artifact families into one provably co-produced set. The loader recomputes raw-file SHA-256 digests for the three tensor artifacts, reads the bank's `model.json`, the gate (`beta.json`), and its sidecar (`beta.meta.json`), then asserts every recorded identity matches the bytes on disk. Any single mismatch aborts with `Model checkpoints, genes, reference bank and fusion weights do not match` — intentionally a single error for the whole web, since any violation means the release is not a unit.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph recomputed["Recomputed at load time"]
        H1["sha(stage1.pt)"]
        H2["sha(stage2.pt)"]
        H3["sha(gene_space.npz)"]
        HG["sha(beta.json)"]
    end
    S1["stage1.pt"]
    S2["stage2.pt"]
    GS["gene_space.npz"]
    BK["bank/model.json"]
    GM["beta.meta.json"]
    G["beta.json"]
    M["release.json sha256 block"]
    S1 -.-> H1
    S2 -.-> H2
    GS -.-> H3
    G -.-> HG
    M -->|equals| H1 & H2 & H3
    BK -->|"checkpoint_sha256 == "| H1
    BK -->|"gene_space_sha256 == "| H3
    GM -->|"checkpoint_sha256 == "| H1
    GM -->|"stage2_checkpoint_sha256 == "| H2
    GM -->|"gene_space_sha256 == "| H3
    GM -->|"cache_fingerprint == bank's"| BK
    GM -->|"gate_sha256 == "| HG
```

Each edge of the web catches a distinct failure mode:

| # | Recorded identity vs. recomputed digest | Failure caught |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `bank.checkpoint_sha256` vs `sha(stage1.pt)` | Bank built from a different alignment checkpoint |
| 2 | `bank.gene_space_sha256` vs `sha(gene_space.npz)` | Bank embeddings in a foreign gene space |
| 3 | `gate_meta.checkpoint_sha256` vs `sha(stage1.pt)` | Gate calibrated on a different Stage-1 model |
| 4 | `gate_meta.stage2_checkpoint_sha256` vs `sha(stage2.pt)` | Gate calibrated against a different expression head |
| 5 | `gate_meta.gene_space_sha256` vs `sha(gene_space.npz)` | Gate fitted under a different gene ordering |
| 6 | `gate_meta.cache_fingerprint` vs `bank.cache_fingerprint` | Gate and bank describe different bank builds |
| 7 | `gate_meta.gate_sha256` vs `sha(beta.json)` | `beta.json` swapped or edited after calibration |

The web closes with two protocol-level consistency checks: the gate metadata's `spatial_context` record must exactly equal the runtime `prediction_protocol()` (a dict covering blocking mode, revision, cell counts, halo radius, seed, and output policy), and the gate's retrieval constants `K` and `tau` must equal the bank's `retrieval_K` and `tau`. Together these guarantee that the fusion weights were fitted under the *same* blocking behavior and *same* neighborhood geometry that inference will use.

Sources: [release.py](/morph2mol/release.py#L27-L45), [spatial_context.py](/predict/spatial_context.py#L81-L90)

## Hash Primitives: Raw Bytes vs Canonical Identity

The system uses two classes of hashing, and the distinction matters. **Raw-file hashes** digest bytes, making them tamper-evident but sensitive to any serialization change. **Canonical hashes** digest a normalized JSON representation, making them stable identity statements about *content* rather than file encodings. Four primitives implement this:

| Primitive | Digests | Canonicalization | Primary consumers |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sha(path)` | Raw file bytes, streamed in 8 MiB blocks | none (byte-exact) | Manifest, binding web, `gate_sha256` |
| `gene_hash(genes)` | Gene symbol list | `json.dumps` of the list | `gene_head_sha256` in Stage-2, gate `fit_signature` |
| `fingerprint(value)` | JSON-serializable dict | `json.dumps` with sorted keys | Bank `cache_fingerprint` |
| `checkpoint_identity(path)` | Raw checkpoint bytes | wrapped as `{'sha256': ...}` | `stage1_identity` embedded in checkpoints |

The streaming implementation matters for the raw hashes: checkpoints and gene spaces are large, so `sha` reads in fixed 8 MiB blocks rather than loading files into memory — verification adds no memory pressure regardless of model size. Canonical hashing is what makes the gene-order binding robust: `gene_head_sha256` inside the Stage-2 checkpoint is compared against `gene_hash` of the gene list *as loaded from the npz*, so a gene space whose rows were reordered — even if the file were re-serialized identically otherwise — cannot pass.

Sources: [retrieval.py](/morph2mol/retrieval.py#L16-L21), [training_contract.py](/morph2mol/training_contract.py#L39-L49), [bank_io.py](/morph2mol/bank_io.py#L30-L31)

## Where Bindings Are Born: Export-Time Verification

Integrity is not only checked at load — it is *constructed* at export. `train/export_release.py` runs its own input-side checks before writing anything, then manufactures the identities that the load-time web will later verify. The export refuses to write into a non-empty directory, eliminating the possibility of stale artifacts mixing into a fresh release.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Load training stage1 + stage2<br/>checkpoints"] --> B["check_stage2_settings<br/>recipe invariants"]
    B --> C{"stage1_identity.sha256 ==<br/>sha source stage1?"}
    C -->|no| X1["Reject: Expression checkpoint<br/>and alignment initializer differ"]
    C -->|yes| D{"gene_head_sha256 ==<br/>gene_hash of exported genes?"}
    D -->|no| X2["Reject: Expression checkpoint<br/>and exported gene order differ"]
    D -->|yes| E["Write stripped stage1.pt<br/>(LoRA tensors only)"]
    E --> F["Write stripped stage2.pt<br/>rebind stage1_identity to<br/>sha of exported stage1.pt"]
    F --> G["Copy gene_space.npz + uni2h"]
    G --> H{"--bank and --beta<br/>supplied together?"}
    H -->|yes| I["Copy bank/, beta.json,<br/>beta.meta.json"]
    H -->|no| J["Non-retrieval release"]
    I --> K["Compute sha256 manifest for<br/>stage1 / stage2 / gene_space"]
    J --> K
    K --> L["Write release.json"]
    L --> M["Self-validate: instantiate<br/>Release(retrieval=...)"]
    M --> N["Print release directory"]
```

> [!TIP]
> Notice the identity rebinding at export: the exporter verifies the *training* Stage-2 checkpoint against the *training* Stage-1 file, but then writes a **stripped** `stage1.pt` (LoRA tensors only, no optimizer state) and re-embeds `stage1_identity` as the hash of the *stripped* file. Since removing optimizer state changes the bytes, the training-time hash would fail every downstream check — the chain must be re-anchored to the artifact that actually ships.

The final step is a fail-fast self-validation: the exporter constructs a full `Release` object against the directory it just wrote, so an export that would fail at load time fails at export time instead. The gate-pairing rule (`--bank` and `--beta` must be supplied together or not at all) prevents half-connected retrieval releases from ever existing.

Sources: [export_release.py](/train/export_release.py#L18-L33), [export_release.py](/train/export_release.py#L45-L64)

## Defense in Depth at Inference Time

Verification executes at three moments during a deployment load, and each layer re-derives checks rather than trusting the previous layer. The CLI entry point first constructs `Release` (layers 1–6). The model constructor then re-checks the *internal* identities of the checkpoints themselves — identities that live inside the `.pt` files and are therefore invisible to manifest-level hashing. Finally, the bank constructor self-verifies when retrieval is initialized.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CLI as predict/predict.py
    participant R as Release (morph2mol/release.py)
    participant M as Morph2Mol (predict/model.py)
    participant B as ReferenceBank (morph2mol/retrieval.py)
    CLI->>R: Release(release_dir, retrieval=not reference)
    R->>R: schema gate, existence, sha256 manifest
    R->>R: 7 cross-artifact binding checks
    R->>R: spatial-context protocol + K/tau consistency
    R-->>CLI: verified paths + hashes dict
    CLI->>M: Morph2Mol(release)
    M->>M: duplicate gene check in gene_space
    M->>M: stage1_identity == release.hashes['stage1']
    M->>M: gene_head_sha256 == gene_hash(loaded genes)
    M->>M: check_stage2_settings on embedded args
    M->>M: load_lora_checked (key set + tensor shapes)
    M->>B: ReferenceBank(bank_dir)
    B->>B: schema, cache_fingerprint, completion marker
    B->>B: retrieval_K == 50 and tau == 0.03
    B-->>M: bank ready for retrieval
```

The model-constructor layer is the subtle one. `Morph2Mol.__init__` re-asserts that the Stage-2 checkpoint's embedded `stage1_identity` equals the release's recomputed Stage-1 hash — catching a swapped `stage1.pt` even if the manifest were regenerated — and re-derives `gene_hash` from the gene space it actually loaded. It then applies **structural** verification to the LoRA adapters: `load_lora_checked` validates that adapter tensor keys are a subset of the encoder's `.A`/`.B` parameters (exactly equal when `complete=True` for Stage-1) and that every tensor shape matches the live module, rejecting checkpoints built for a different adapter configuration before any state is copied.

Sources: [predict.py](/predict/predict.py#L60-L61), [model.py](/predict/model.py#L14-L34), [training_contract.py](/morph2mol/training_contract.py#L68-L77)

## The Reference Bank as a Self-Verifying Artifact

Because the bank directory is copied wholesale into the release, its integrity is maintained independently of the manifest through a construction protocol in `ReferenceBank.__init__`. The checks run in a strict order: schema whitelist; a **content fingerprint** — `cache_fingerprint` is the `fingerprint()` of the entire `model.json` minus the fingerprint field itself, so any edit to the bank's description (objects, hyperparameters, protocol ids) invalidates it; fixed retrieval constants (`target_size == 100`, `retrieval_K == 50`, `tau == 0.03`); an exact object count; and a **completion marker** — `bank_complete.json` must exist, report the same object count, and carry the same cache fingerprint, which makes partially built or partially copied banks detectable at load.

Per-object feature files are bound separately by `validate_feature`, which requires each object's metadata `checkpoint_sha256` and `feature_protocol_id` to match the bank model's, enforces the 1536-dimensional raw Phase-1 feature contract, and rejects anything that is not the `phase1` output field — preventing Stage-2 expression vectors from being ingested as retrieval keys.

Sources: [retrieval.py](/morph2mol/retrieval.py#L82-L100), [bank_io.py](/morph2mol/bank_io.py#L58-L65)

## Closing the Loop: Calibration-Time Evidence

The binding web only works because the gate-fitting stage manufactures its side of the web under verification itself. `train/fit_beta.py` instantiates `Release(retrieval=False)` for the model side, then manually binds the *source* bank to the release by comparing `model.json`'s checkpoint and gene-space hashes against the release hashes — the same edges the load-time web will later assert. Reference slides used for calibration must themselves be verifiable: each calibration input's stored prediction metadata (read via `prediction_metadata`, tolerating both key namespaces) must carry a `spatial_context` record equal to the runtime protocol and `stage1_sha256` / `stage2_sha256` values equal to the release hashes — meaning **slide outputs double as evidence artifacts** that testify which model produced them.

The emitted gate is stamped with `fit_signature.genes = gene_hash(genes)`, and the sidecar `beta.meta.json` records everything the binding web will consume: `gate_sha256`, all three checkpoint hashes, the bank's `cache_fingerprint`, the retrieval constants, and the full spatial-context protocol. This is the genesis of every edge in the web — nothing at load time is trusted that was not written under a verified identity at fit time.

Sources: [fit_beta.py](/train/fit_beta.py#L28-L35), [fit_beta.py](/train/fit_beta.py#L50-L56), [fit_beta.py](/train/fit_beta.py#L86-L99), [prediction_io.py](/morph2mol/prediction_io.py#L4-L7)

## Coverage and Residual Risk

No verification design is total, and this one makes its trade-offs explicit. The table below maps each artifact family to its mechanism, the strength of the guarantee, and what remains outside the guarantee:

| Artifact family | Mechanism | Guarantee strength | Explicitly not covered |
|---|---|---|---|
| `stage1.pt`, `stage2.pt`, `gene_space.npz` | Manifest sha256 + checkpoint-embedded identities | Byte-tamper-evident where manifest entries exist | Manifest entries are optional — absent entries skip the file check |
| `uni2h/` encoder directory | Existence check only | Path presence | No content hash; contents assumed immutable |
| `bank/` directory | Content fingerprint + completion marker + per-object `validate_feature` | Build-level and description-level integrity | Individual matrix files are not byte-hashed |
| `beta.json` | `gate_sha256` in sidecar meta | Byte-exact binding | The sidecar itself is bound only indirectly |
| `release.json` | Schema gate | Format safety | The manifest is unsigned — it must originate from the exporter |

> [!TIP]
> The manifest's `sha256` block is enforced only for entries that are present (`if expected and expected != ...`). This is why the design layers *checkpoint-embedded* identities (Stage-2's `stage1_identity`, `gene_head_sha256`) on top of the manifest: a tampered or hand-written manifest cannot make mismatched tensors load, because the tensors carry their own binding evidence inside the file bytes.

Sources: [release.py](/morph2mol/release.py#L21-L26), [model.py](/predict/model.py#L21-L27)

## Failure Catalog

Because every check fails with a specific message, verification failures are diagnosable from the error text alone. The catalog below maps each message to the check that raised it and the most likely operational cause:

| Error message | Raised by | Likely cause |
|---|---|---|
| `Unsupported release.json schema` | Schema gate | Pointing at a non-release directory or a foreign format |
| `Missing release artifact <key>: <path>` | Existence check | Incomplete copy; artifact renamed or omitted |
| `Release checksum mismatch: <key>` | Manifest sha256 | Artifact regenerated or replaced after export |
| `Model checkpoints, genes, reference bank and fusion weights do not match` | Binding web (any of 7 edges) | Mixing artifacts from different runs |
| `Fusion calibration and spatial prediction settings differ` | Protocol pin | Gate fitted under a different blocking revision |
| `Fusion weights and reference bank retrieval settings differ` | K/tau consistency | Gate fitted against a bank with other retrieval constants |
| `Stage-2 was trained with another Stage-1 initializer` | `stage1_identity` re-check | Swapped `stage1.pt` |
| `Stage-2 gene order mismatch` | `gene_head_sha256` | `gene_space.npz` from another run |
| `Stage-2 gene-head order differs from this run` / LoRA key/shape mismatch | Training-side contract checks | Cross-run checkpoint reuse during training |
| `Bank model fingerprint mismatch` | `cache_fingerprint` | Hand-edited `model.json` |
| `Bank has not completed all objects` | Completion marker | Partially built or partially copied bank |

Sources: [release.py](/morph2mol/release.py#L10-L45), [model.py](/predict/model.py#L19-L34), [retrieval.py](/morph2mol/retrieval.py#L88-L100), [training_contract.py](/morph2mol/training_contract.py#L61-L77)

## Where to Go Next

The verification system sits at the boundary between several subsystems, and each has a dedicated page: see how the artifacts themselves are produced in [Model Export and Release Packaging](17-model-export-and-release-packaging), how the gate side of the binding web behaves mathematically in [Gated Fusion Weights](12-gated-fusion-weights), what the pinned spatial-context protocol controls in [Spatial Context Blocking](19-spatial-context-blocking), and how the bank's retrieval constants are used at query time in [Cluster Retrieval Mechanics](11-cluster-retrieval-mechanics). For how prediction outputs become the evidence artifacts consumed at calibration, continue to [Streaming Output and Fault Tolerance](20-streaming-output-and-fault-tolerance).
